items.title: Bromwich inversion formula
items.description: Response derives the density of states by starting from Q(β) = ∫_0^∞ dE e^{-βE} g(E) and obtains g(E) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\beta'-i\infty}^{\beta'+i\infty} dβ \, e^{+βE} Q(β) with a positive sign in the exponent, recognizing this as the Bromwich inversion of the Laplace transform.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly provides this formula with β' notation and the e^{+βE} kernel.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes the formula with e^{-βE} (copying the forward transform sign) or omits the 1/(2πi) prefactor.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core derivation and final equation; reference answer requires this exact formula.

items.title: Q as Laplace transform
items.description: Response identifies the partition function Q(β) = ∫_0^∞ dE e^{-βE} g(E) as the forward Laplace transform of the density of states g(E), which is the premise that enables inversion to obtain g(E).

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts correctly identified this relationship; it is the foundational step the entire derivation depends on.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats the integral as a Fourier transform or fails to connect it to the Laplace transform structure.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Foundational step; without it the Bromwich inversion has no justification.

items.title: Beta physical meaning
items.description: Response explains the significance of the variables by stating that β equals 1/(k_B T), carries units of inverse energy, and serves as the Laplace conjugate to E in the partition function equation.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed β = 1/(k_B T) with units 1/energy; some also noted the Laplace-conjugate role, which deepens the connection to the inversion.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states β is inverse temperature without noting its role as the Laplace conjugate variable or its units.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly addresses the sub-question on variable significance.

items.title: g(E) significance
items.description: Response explains the significance of g(E) as the density of states representing the number of microstates per unit energy, with units of 1/energy.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) requires the significance of variables; all rollouts identified g(E) as density of states with units 1/energy.
provenance.discriminates: A response that calls g(E) dimensionless or gives it units of 1/energy², or fails to describe it as states per unit energy.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses variable-significance sub-question; central to the derivation.

items.title: Complex analysis role
items.description: Response discusses the role of complex analysis by stating that β is analytically continued into the complex plane, the inverse Laplace transform is performed as a contour integral, and the residue theorem or contour deformation is used to evaluate it, recognizing that poles of Q(β) encode the energy spectrum.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollouts 1 and 3 explicitly used residue calculations; Rollout 2 used a series approach that de-emphasized contour mechanics. The reference and question both emphasize complex analysis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that inverts the transform purely by series expansion without invoking residue calculus or contour deformation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Merged three overlapping sub-question items on complex analysis role.

items.title: Quantum Q(beta) form
items.description: Response writes the quantum harmonic oscillator partition function as Q(β) = e^{-βℏω/2}/(1 - e^{-βℏω}) with the zero-point energy prefactor included.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollouts 1 and 2 retained zero-point energy throughout; Rollout 3 derived primarily without it. The physical convention includes the zero-point term.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes Q(β) = 1/(1 - e^{-βℏω}) without the e^{-βℏω/2} prefactor, shifting all energy levels down by ℏω/2.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate quantity for obtaining the quantum density of states.

items.title: Correct pole locations
items.description: Response states that the poles of Q(β) for the quantum harmonic oscillator occur at β_n = 2πin/(ℏω) for n ∈ ℤ\{0}, arising from 1 - e^{-βℏω} = 0, and avoids placing poles on the real axis or inserting a spurious extra factor of i.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts correctly identified pole locations; this is a load-bearing intermediate result for the residue calculation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that places poles on the real axis at β_n = 2πn/(ℏω) or inserts an extra factor of i giving β_n = i·2πin/(ℏω).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Load-bearing intermediate; pitfall of wrong pole locations absorbed.

items.title: Contour closure direction
items.description: Avoids closing the Bromwich contour to the right for E > 0, instead stating that the contour closes to the left where e^{βE} decays during inverting the Laplace transform, enclosing all poles of Q(β).

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Contour closure direction' (severity medium): closing to the right for E > 0 yields g(E) = 0.
provenance.discriminates: A response that closes the contour to the right for E > 0 or fails to specify closure direction at all.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed pitfall; directional error in contour closure.

items.title: Classical vs quantum g(E)
items.description: Response distinguishes between the classical density of states g_cl(E) = 1/(ℏω) for E > 0 and the quantum harmonic oscillator result g(E) = Σ_n δ(E - (n+1/2)ℏω), reflecting the quantized energy levels.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts that addressed the quantum case derived this delta-function comb; it is the concrete result of the inversion for the quantum oscillator.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives a smooth or continuous g(E) for the quantum case instead of a discrete delta-function spectrum.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Merged two items on the final quantum delta-comb result.

items.title: E variable significance
items.description: Response explains the significance of E as the energy integration variable ranging from 0 to ∞ in the partition function integral, consistent with the lower limit of the Laplace transform.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) asks for variable significance; the integration range and role of E is a required part.
provenance.discriminates: A response that does not mention the energy range E ≥ 0 or the role of E as the integration variable in the transform.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses variable-significance sub-question.

items.title: Dimensional consistency
items.description: Response notes that Q(β) is dimensionless and that the measure \frac{dβ}{2πi} in the \int for inverting the Laplace transform carries units of 1/energy, making g(E) dimensionally consistent.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Variable significance incomplete' (severity low): noting dimensional consistency across the transform pair.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns g(E) wrong dimensions or ignores how the Bromwich measure carries units of 1/energy.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth; verifies the Bromwich formula output.

items.title: Residue value correct
items.description: Response states that each residue of \frac{1}{1 - e^{-βℏω}} at a pole β_n equals 1/(ℏω), arising from the chain-rule derivative of the denominator during inverting the Laplace transform.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Residue coefficient wrong' (severity high): forgetting the ℏω derivative factor gives residues of (-1)^n instead of 1/(ℏω).
provenance.discriminates: A response that computes residues by evaluating only the numerator at the pole, yielding (-1)^n instead of 1/(ℏω).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate result for evaluating the contour integral.

items.title: Contour parameter choice
items.description: Response states that β' (or equivalent contour parameter γ) in the Bromwich integral is chosen to the right of all singularities of Q(β) in the complex β-plane.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference uses β' notation; the requirement that it lie to the right of all singularities is implicit in the Bromwich formula.
provenance.discriminates: A response that places the contour to the left of singularities or does not specify the constraint on the contour's real part.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Necessary condition for the validity of the Bromwich inversion.

items.title: No classical-only answer
items.description: Avoids presenting only the classical flat density of states 1/(ℏω) as the complete answer for the harmonic oscillator without acknowledging the quantum delta-function comb.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Classical–quantum conflation' (severity medium): the classical result is simpler but incomplete if the quantum spectrum is expected.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives g(E) = 1/(ℏω) as the sole final answer without mentioning quantized energy levels.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed pitfall; omits the quantum result entirely.

items.title: Series alone insufficient
items.description: Avoids inverting Q(β) by a purely term-by-term series expansion without any reference to complex analysis, contour integration, or the residue theorem.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Series approach evades complex analysis': the series method is valid but does not address sub-question (c) about the role of complex analysis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that expands Q(β) = Σ e^{-βε_n} and identifies each term as a delta function, with no mention of the Bromwich contour or residues.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed pitfall; sidesteps the complex-analysis role asked for.

items.title: Q(beta) significance
items.description: Response explains the significance of Q(β) as the canonical partition function, which is dimensionless and encodes the thermodynamic properties of the harmonic oscillator.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) asks for the significance of variables including Q(β); all rollouts identified it as the partition function.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions Q(β) without explaining it is the partition function or its role in the canonical ensemble.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses variable-significance sub-question for β's conjugate quantity.

items.title: Polypeptide mass numerator
items.description: The response uses the polypeptide mass value of 65,760 daltons as the numerator in the amino acid count calculation.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly uses 65,760 daltons as the dividend in the first step.
provenance.discriminates: A response that misreads the mass value or uses a different number.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Load-bearing input; without correct numerator the 480 residue count fails.

items.title: Divides by 137
items.description: The response divides 65,760 daltons by 137 daltons per amino acid to obtain the residue count without subtracting water mass from the average.

provenance.evidence_detail: The water-loss mass correction pitfall warns against adjusting 137 Da downward to ~119 Da; the reference uses 137 directly.
provenance.discriminates: A response that subtracts ~18 Da for water loss and uses ~119 Da as the divisor, yielding ~553 residues.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key divisor choice; absorbs the water-loss-correction pitfall observed in collective errors.

items.title: Amino acid count 480
items.description: The response computes the polypeptide length as 480 amino acids from dividing 65,760 by 137.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer's first step is 65,760 / 137 = 480 amino acids.
provenance.discriminates: A response that skips the division or uses a wrong divisor producing a different residue count.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Central intermediate result; all downstream calculations depend on it.

items.title: Equal composition assumption
items.description: The response applies the assumption that the polypeptide contains equal amounts of all 20 amino acids to justify using the 137 dalton average directly.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus_correct section notes that the equal-composition assumption validates using 137 Da as the mean residue mass.
provenance.discriminates: A response that ignores the assumption or argues the average mass cannot be applied without sequence information.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Stated modelling assumption that makes the average mass applicable; required for correctness.

items.title: Triplet codon stated
items.description: The response states that each amino acid is encoded by a codon of three nucleotides.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts and the reference agree on the triplet genetic code as the basis for multiplying by 3.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a non-triplet mapping or fails to mention the codon structure.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required biological principle bridging residue count to nucleotide count.

items.title: Multiplies by three
items.description: The response multiplies the 480 amino acid count by three nucleotides per amino acid to convert to nucleotides.

provenance.evidence_detail: The codon factor inverted pitfall identifies dividing 480 by 3 as a high-severity error.
provenance.discriminates: A response that divides 480 by 3 and reports 160 nucleotides.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core conversion step; absorbs the divide-by-three pitfall that yields 160.

items.title: Final 1440 nucleotides
items.description: The response states the mRNA length as 1440 nucleotides.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer's final result is 1,440 nucleotides (480 amino acids × 3 nucleotides per amino acid).
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives 480, 160, 1,443, or any other value as the final nucleotide count.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The requested final quantity; without it the answer is incomplete.

items.title: Coding region specified
items.description: The response specifies the 1440 nucleotides as the coding region of the mRNA rather than the total molecule length.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer specifies 'the coding region of the mRNA would have to be 1,440 nucleotides long.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels 1,440 as the total mRNA length without distinguishing the coding region.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Distinguishes coding from total mRNA; prevents over-claiming about full molecule length.

items.title: No stop or UTR addition
items.description: Avoids adding extra nucleotides for a stop codon or untranslated regions to the 1440 nucleotide coding region total.

provenance.evidence_detail: The stop/UTR overcomplication pitfall identifies adding 3 nt for a stop codon or UTR lengths as an out-of-scope correction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that adds 3 nt for a stop codon to get 1,443 or adds UTR estimates to reach ~1,540–1,640.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed pitfall where responses inflated the coding region with non-coding segments.

items.title: No 480 as nucleotide count
items.description: Avoids presenting 480 as the mRNA length in nucleotides rather than as an amino acid count.

provenance.evidence_detail: The residue count as answer pitfall describes stopping at 480 and presenting it as the final length.
provenance.discriminates: A response whose final stated mRNA length is 480 with no nucleotide conversion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed confusion between residue count and nucleotide count in flawed responses.

items.title: Physical length optional
items.description: The response optionally converts 1440 nucleotides to a physical length of approximately 490 nm using 0.34 nm per nucleotide.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts included the physical length conversion, but the reference does not require it; it is defensible as an extension.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives only 490 nm with no 1,440 nucleotide count would fail to match the reference's required output.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth beyond the requested quantity; not required for correctness.

items.title: Methylamine proton acceptor
items.description: The response states that CH3NH2 acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base that accepts a proton from H2O.

provenance.evidence_detail: Part (a) requires the chemical mechanism linking methylamine's behavior to litmus turning blue.
provenance.discriminates: A response that only says 'it is a base' without specifying proton acceptance from water.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core conceptual requirement for part (a); without it the explanation of blue litmus fails.

items.title: Hydroxide equilibrium
items.description: The response gives the equilibrium CH3NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3NH3+ + OH- using equilibrium arrows rather than a single forward arrow.

provenance.evidence_detail: Part (a) target requires the OH--producing equilibrium as the link to litmus blue.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names the base but omits the equation producing OH-.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific equation with ⇌ is the load-bearing intermediate result for part (a).

items.title: OH- turns litmus blue
items.description: The response identifies OH- as the species that causes litmus to turn blue in the CH3NH2 solution.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts linked OH- production to the litmus color change.
provenance.discriminates: A response giving the equilibrium but never connecting OH- to the blue litmus observation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly links the equilibrium product to the observed phenomenon the question asks about.

items.title: pKb value stated
items.description: The response includes the pKb value of 3.36 for methylamine.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference provides pKb = 3.36, which no rollout included.
provenance.discriminates: A response missing the specific numeric pKb value given in the reference.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds quantitative precision but is not required to explain the litmus observation.

items.title: Weak base stronger than water
items.description: The response states that methylamine is a weak base but a stronger base than water.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference includes the comparative claim that methylamine is a stronger base than water, which rollouts omitted.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels methylamine a base without the explicit comparison to water.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Provides the comparative rationale for why the equilibrium produces OH-, adding depth.

items.title: Aniline protonation by HCl
items.description: The response states that C6H5NH2 is protonated by HCl to form the cation C6H5NH3+.

provenance.evidence_detail: Part (b) requires identifying the protonation reaction of aniline with HCl.
provenance.discriminates: A response attributing dissolution to hydrogen bonding or polarity instead of protonation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core mechanism for part (b); correct dissolution explanation depends on this protonation.

items.title: Anilinium chloride product
items.description: The response identifies the product as anilinium chloride with the formula C6H5NH3+Cl-.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly labels the product as anilinium chloride next to the formula.
provenance.discriminates: A response giving only the formula without the name anilinium chloride.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Naming both the salt and its formula is the specific required product for part (b).

items.title: Salt is water-soluble
items.description: The response states that the salt C6H5NH3+Cl- formed in part (b) is water-soluble.

provenance.evidence_detail: Medium-severity mined pitfall: identified product but no solubility link.
provenance.discriminates: A response giving the correct equation but never connecting the ionic salt to dissolution in water.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Solubility of the salt is the direct answer to why aniline dissolves in aqueous HCl.

items.title: Part (b) reaction equation
items.description: The response gives a reaction equation for C6H5NH2 with HCl or with H3O+ and Cl- yielding C6H5NH3+Cl-.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollouts differed on representation (HCl vs H3O+ + Cl-); the reference uses H3O+ + Cl- but all valid forms are equivalent.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names the product but provides no reaction equation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Concrete equation formalises the protonation; important but subordinate to the conceptual explanation.

items.title: Avoids reversed proton transfer
items.description: Avoids writing CH3NH2 as a proton donor to water, which would incorrectly produce H3O+ and a deprotonated nitrogen species.

provenance.evidence_detail: High-severity mined pitfall: reversed proton transfer in part (a).
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes CH3NH2 + H2O → CH3NH– + H3O+, reversing the acid-base roles.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific error direction for part (a); caught by naming the exact wrong arrow.

items.title: Salt not hydrogen bonding
items.description: Avoids attributing the dissolution of C6H5NH2 in HCl to hydrogen bonding or polarity, and instead attributes it to formation of the C6H5NH3+Cl- salt.

provenance.evidence_detail: High-severity mined pitfall: wrong solubility mechanism via hydrogen bonding.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says aniline dissolves because it hydrogen-bonds with water.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common wrong mechanism for part (b); naming the correct alternative increases checkability.

items.title: Avoids resonance-blocks-protonation
items.description: Avoids claiming that the nitrogen lone pair in C6H5NH2 is too delocalised by resonance to be protonated by HCl.

provenance.evidence_detail: Medium-severity mined pitfall: over-extrapolating aniline resonance to deny protonation.
provenance.discriminates: A response asserting aniline cannot be protonated because of resonance delocalisation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Plausible-sounding but incorrect claim that aniline cannot be protonated; addresses a specific misconception.

items.title: Final answer 900 ml
items.description: The response states the volume of water to be added is 900 ml and selects option (d).

provenance.evidence_detail: The MCQ requires selecting one of (a)–(d); the correct answer is (d) 900 ml.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that pick (a), (b), or (c) due to miscalculation or misreading.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correctness collapses without the right answer; directly anchored to the question's requested quantity.

items.title: Alpha formula
items.description: The response uses the relationship alpha = sqrt(Ka / C) (equivalently alpha is proportional to 1/sqrt(C)) for the degree of dissociation of acetic acid.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts and the reference rely on α ∝ √(Ka/C); the mined pitfall flags dropping the square root.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that assume a linear relationship alpha ∝ 1/C (or alpha ∝ V).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Load-bearing formula from which all downstream results follow; no correct derivation without it.

items.title: Doubling needs 4x dilution
items.description: The response states that doubling the degree of dissociation alpha requires quadrupling the volume (or quartering the concentration), derived from alpha being proportional to sqrt(V).

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus: α₂ = 2α₁ ⟹ V₂ = 4V₁; this is the conceptual core of the derivation.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that claim doubling alpha requires only doubling the volume.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning step converting the doubling condition into the 4x dilution factor.

items.title: V2 = 1200 ml
items.description: The response derives the final total volume V2 = 4 times 300 = 1200 ml.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference and all correct rollouts establish V2 = 4 × V1 from the square-root dependence; this is the load-bearing step.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that set V2 = 2 × 300 = 600 ml by assuming linear scaling.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate result; every wrong option diverges from this value.

items.title: Subtracts initial volume
items.description: The response performs the subtraction water added = 1200 - 300 = 900 ml and avoids presenting 1200 ml as the volume of water added.

provenance.evidence_detail: The mined pitfall 'Final volume as answer' flags reporting V2 = 1200 ml directly instead of subtracting the initial 300 ml.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that stop at V2 = 1200 ml and never compute the water added.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common pitfall is reporting 1200 without subtracting 300; subtraction is essential for correctness.

items.title: Final concentration 0.05 M
items.description: The response states or uses the final concentration C2 = 0.05 M (i.e., 0.2 M divided by 4).

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts: doubling α requires C2 = C1/4 = 0.05 M.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that compute C2 = 0.1 M by halving instead of quartering.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Valid alternative intermediate that confirms the 4x dilution; strong discriminative value.

items.title: Uses given initial values
items.description: The response uses the initial concentration 0.2 M, initial volume 300 ml, and conserved moles of acetic acid (0.2 times 0.300 = 0.060 mol) as given values.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts anchor the calculation to V1 = 300 ml and C1 = 0.2 M from the prompt.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that misread the initial volume or concentration.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Anchors the calculation to the problem data; ensures dilution direction is toward larger volume.

items.title: Uses Ka value
items.description: The response uses the given Ka value of 1.8 x 10^-5 for acetic acid in the dissociation calculation.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question supplies Ka = 1.8 × 10^-5; the reference and rollouts employ it in the sqrt(Ka/C) expression.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that omit Ka entirely or use an incorrect value.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real but not decisive; Ka cancels in the ratio so it is confirmatory rather than load-bearing.

items.title: Avoids linear scaling
items.description: Avoids assuming a linear relationship between alpha and volume that would yield V2 = 600 ml and water added = 300 ml, corresponding to option (b).

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Linear instead of square-root' (high severity) produces exactly this wrong path: doubling V instead of quadrupling.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that pick (b) 300 ml or derive V2 = 600 ml via linear proportionality.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly targets the observed distractor option (b); specific wrong move named.

items.title: Avoids alpha vs H+ confusion
items.description: Avoids substituting the hydrogen ion concentration [H+] = sqrt(Ka times C) in place of the degree of dissociation alpha = sqrt(Ka / C).

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confusing α with [H⁺]' (medium severity): swapping which quantity scales with which power of C.
provenance.discriminates: Responses that set up the proportionality using [H⁺] ∝ √C instead of alpha ∝ 1/√C.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Conceptual trap specific to weak-acid dilution; less frequently observed so lower weight.

items.title: Framework independent of interactions
items.description: States that the equilibrium statistical mechanics framework applies to strongly-correlated systems because its key assumptions do not require weak interactions.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agree and the reference supports that equilibrium validity does not depend on interaction strength.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims strong correlations automatically place a system outside equilibrium statistical mechanics.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core thesis; directly answers why equilibrium treatment is valid regardless of interaction strength.

items.title: Partition function exact for any H
items.description: States that Z = Tr e^{-βH} is exact for any Hamiltonian including strongly interacting ones, so the equilibrium partition function remains valid for strongly-correlated systems.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim that the partition function formula is exact regardless of interaction strength.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts the partition function breaks down when interactions are strong.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Concrete formula anchoring the central claim; load-bearing for the entire argument.

items.title: Temperature as central concept
items.description: Identifies the existence of a well-defined temperature as the central concept determining whether equilibrium statistical mechanics applies to a system's behavior.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference highlights 'the concept of temperature' as the focal point, which the rollouts treated as merely one assumption among several.
provenance.discriminates: A response that lists many assumptions without identifying temperature as the load-bearing organizing idea.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects the question's focus on temperature to the applicability of equilibrium mechanics.

items.title: Thermalization determines equilibrium
items.description: States that a well-defined temperature and partition function depend on thermalization rather than interaction strength per se, making thermalization the assumption that connects interactions to equilibrium validity for strongly-correlated systems.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus claim across all rollouts; also matches the implicit constraint about temperature and partition function depending on thermalization.
provenance.discriminates: A response that ties the existence of temperature to weak coupling.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning bridging interactions and equilibrium; addresses the disputed causal point.

items.title: Strong interactions facilitate thermalization
items.description: States that strong interactions lead to thermalization rather than hindering it, consistent with the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, for strongly-correlated systems.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Reversing interaction-thermalization causality' warns against claiming strong correlations prevent thermalization.
provenance.discriminates: A response that reverses the causal direction, claiming strong interactions disrupt thermalization.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses the disputed point on interaction directionality; important without being essential.

items.title: Avoids conflating correlation with non-equilibrium
items.description: Avoids claiming that strongly-correlated systems are out of equilibrium or cannot be described by equilibrium ensembles because interactions are strong, which reverses the thermalization causality suggested by the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Correlations ≠ non-equilibrium' (severity: high) identifies conflation of strong correlations with non-equilibrium status.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats 'strongly correlated' as synonymous with 'non-equilibrium.'
provenance.calibration_rationale: Traps observed in flawed responses; covers the specific false inference about interactions and equilibrium.

items.title: Distinguishes approximation from framework failure
items.description: Explicitly distinguishes between the failure of perturbative or mean-field approximations for strongly-correlated systems and the continued validity of equilibrium statistical mechanics itself.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confusing perturbation with framework' (severity: high) identifies this conflation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that equates failure of weak-coupling approximations with failure of the equilibrium framework itself.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core distinction; without it the entire answer collapses into conflating method failure with framework failure.

items.title: Lists statistical mechanics assumptions
items.description: Identifies at least two assumptions of statistical mechanics relevant to strongly-correlated systems, such as ergodicity, ensemble equivalence, thermalization, or separation of timescales.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question b asks to identify and discuss the assumptions of statistical mechanics bearing on equilibrium use.
provenance.discriminates: A response that never names any specific assumption of statistical mechanics.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Grounds the argument in named assumptions; addresses the question's explicit focus on assumptions.

items.title: Notes equilibrium failure cases
items.description: Acknowledges that equilibrium breaks down in specific regimes of strongly-correlated systems such as many-body localization, integrability, or glassiness, placing limits on the framework's applicability.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Omitting equilibrium failure cases' (severity: medium) flags one-sided answers that never note boundary conditions.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims equilibrium always applies without noting genuine exceptions.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds necessary nuance about when equilibrium conditions do not hold; names specific physical mechanisms.

items.title: Reservoir contact or fixed constraints
items.description: States that equilibrium statistical mechanics requires the system to be in thermal contact with a reservoir or isolated with fixed macroscopic constraints, not weak interactions.

provenance.evidence_detail: Implicit constraint: equilibrium requires reservoir contact or isolation with fixed macroscopic constraints, not weak interactions.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits the physical setup required for equilibrium.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Identifies the actual physical conditions for equilibrium; directly counters the weak-interaction misconception.

items.title: Non-perturbative methods exist
items.description: Mentions at least one non-perturbative method used to compute equilibrium properties of strongly-correlated systems, such as DMFT, QMC, tensor networks, or RG.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollouts diverged on which non-perturbative methods to list; all mentioned at least one, and the reference is silent, so any correct method name suffices.
provenance.discriminates: A response that implies no calculational tools exist for strongly-correlated equilibrium problems.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth; demonstrates that practical computation of equilibrium properties is feasible.

items.title: Strong correlations produce novel phases
items.description: Notes that strong interactions produce novel equilibrium phases in strongly-correlated systems, such as Mott insulators, heavy fermions, or unconventional superconductors.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts give overlapping lists of equilibrium phases arising from strong correlations.
provenance.discriminates: A response that implies strong correlations only cause calculational difficulty without producing new equilibrium physics.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds concrete examples of equilibrium behavior in strongly-correlated systems; supporting depth.

items.title: Synthesizes why equilibrium is used
items.description: Synthesizes the assumptions, the implications of interactions, and the conditions for thermalization into an overall argument for why equilibrium is used for strongly-correlated systems.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question d requires synthesizing the reasoning into a coherent answer to the 'why' question.
provenance.discriminates: A response that lists facts without connecting them to answer why equilibrium treatment is justified.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Integrative criterion; without synthesis the answer remains a list rather than a coherent argument.

items.title: Mother genotype Ssaa
items.description: The response states the mother's genotype as Ssaa.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference answer gives mother's genotype as Ssaa.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns the mother a different genotype such as SsAa, SSAa, or ssaa.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without this the response is wrong.

items.title: Father genotype SsAa
items.description: The response states the father's genotype as SsAa.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference answer gives father's genotype as SsAa.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns the father a different genotype such as SSAa, SsAA, or ssAa.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without this the response is wrong.

items.title: Two independently assorting loci
items.description: The response identifies two independently assorting loci for coat coloration, one for color (A/a) and one for pattern (S/s), applying Mendelian independent assortment.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Single-locus collapse' — treating color and spotting as one gene.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats all three phenotypes as products of a single locus with multiple alleles or incomplete dominance.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Framework for the entire cross; load-bearing for all reasoning.

items.title: Black dominant over tan
items.description: The response states that the black allele A is dominant over the tan allele a at the color locus.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed that black (A) is dominant over tan (a).
provenance.discriminates: A response that reverses dominance or fails to assign dominance at the color locus.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required to infer parental and offspring genotypes correctly.

items.title: Solid dominant over spotted
items.description: The response states that the solid allele S is dominant over the spotted allele s at the pattern locus.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed that solid (S) is dominant over spotted (s).
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns spotting as dominant, which would make both solid parents homozygous recessive.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required to infer that spotted pups must be ss.

items.title: Both parents Ss at pattern
items.description: The response explains that the spotted black pup requires both parents to be heterozygous Ss at the pattern locus, since each solid parent must contribute a recessive s allele.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed both parents are Ss because a spotted offspring (ss) from two solid parents requires each parent to carry s.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns one or both parents as SS at the pattern locus, which cannot produce a spotted pup.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning step linking phenotype to parental genotype.

items.title: Father Aa from tan offspring
items.description: The response explains that the 2 solid tan pups require the solid black father to carry the recessive tan allele a, making him Aa at the color locus.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed the father must be heterozygous Aa because tan offspring (aa) require an a allele from the father.
provenance.discriminates: A response that leaves the father as homozygous AA, which cannot produce tan offspring.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning step for father's genotype at color locus.

items.title: Mother aa from tan phenotype
items.description: The response explains that the solid tan mother is homozygous aa at the color locus because tan is recessive and only aa expresses the tan phenotype.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed the mother is aa because her tan phenotype requires homozygosity for the recessive allele.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns the tan mother a heterozygous Aa genotype, which would make her phenotypically black.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning step for mother's genotype at color locus.

items.title: Expected ratio and observed fit
items.description: The response states that the cross Ssaa × SsAa produces an expected phenotypic ratio of approximately 3 solid tan : 3 solid black : 1 spotted tan : 1 spotted black, and confirms the observed 2:2:1 pups are consistent with this ratio.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed the expected ratio from Ssaa × SsAa is 3:3:1:1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that predicts a different ratio such as 1:1:1:1 or 3:1.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Validates the genotypes against observed phenotypes.

items.title: Missing spotted-tan explained
items.description: The response notes that the absence of spotted tan pups among the 5 offspring is consistent with the small sample size, since the expected count of spotted tan is less than one pup.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Over-reading small N' — treating the missing spotted-tan as requiring a special genetic mechanism.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats the absence of spotted tan as genetically impossible or requiring an explanation beyond sampling variance.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses the obvious objection; prevents over-interpretation.

items.title: Allele symbols defined
items.description: The response defines the allele symbols for coat coloration as A (black), a (tan), S (solid), and s (spotted) before or alongside the genotypes of the parents.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference answer provides genotypes using A/a and S/s notation but does not define the symbols; a complete answer must.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses allele symbols without ever defining which phenotype each represents.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Makes the genotypes unambiguous and checkable.

items.title: Mendelian segregation applied
items.description: The response applies the principle of Mendelian segregation by stating that each parent contributes one allele per locus to each offspring.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question b demands application of Mendelian genetics principles, including segregation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states genotypes without invoking segregation to explain how recessive alleles are passed to offspring.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects reasoning to requested Mendelian principles.

items.title: Gametes and Punnett square
items.description: The response identifies the mother's gametes as Sa and sa, the father's gametes as SA, Sa, sA, and sa, and shows a Punnett square or gamete table listing the offspring genotypes.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference cross Ssaa × SsAa implies the mother produces Sa and sa gametes; a detailed derivation requires this step.
provenance.discriminates: A response that lists incorrect maternal gametes such as SA and sa.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds depth; not strictly necessary for correct genotypes.

items.title: Offspring genotype classes
items.description: The response groups the offspring phenotypes into genotype classes: S_aa for solid tan, S_A_ for solid black, and ssA_ for spotted black pups.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts derived that the spotted offspring must be ss and the black offspring must carry A.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns the spotted black pup a genotype inconsistent with ss at pattern or lacks A at color.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Links each observed phenotype to its underlying genotype.

items.title: Avoids epistasis for missing spotted-tan
items.description: The response avoids introducing epistasis, linkage, or a restriction of spotting to black coats specifically to eliminate the spotted tan phenotype from the pups.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Over-reading small N' — introducing epistasis to force the absence of spotted-tan.
provenance.discriminates: A response that fabricates an epistatic interaction (e.g., spotting only visible on black) to explain why no spotted tan pups appear.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common wrong move; sample size alone explains the absence.

items.title: Spotted-tan probability 1/8
items.description: The response states that the probability of a spotted tan pup from the cross Ssaa × SsAa is 1/8.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts derived the 3:3:1:1 ratio, where spotted tan is 1/8 of offspring.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns a different probability for spotted tan offspring.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Quantifies the expected absence; adds precision.

items.title: Particle gains KE
items.description: States the particle gains kinetic energy and begins to move due to the energy added by heating the metal tray.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) asks for a qualitative description of the particle's motion after heating; reference says 'particle will move due to the energy added by heating.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims the particle stays motionless or that no energy reaches the particle.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core claim of the answer; without it the response misses the primary physical outcome.

items.title: Joule heating mechanism
items.description: States the electric force heats the metal tray via Joule heating and the particle gains energy through contact with or radiation from the heated tray, not through direct electrostatic acceleration.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Electric force on particle' — correct result: the electric force heats the tray (Joule heating); the particle then gains energy through thermal contact or radiation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits the Joule-heating mechanism or says the electric force acts on the particle directly.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct causal chain from electric force to particle motion; important intermediate reasoning.

items.title: Initially at rest
items.description: States the particle is initially at rest at absolute zero, corresponding to zero classical kinetic energy, and that subsequent heating changes this state.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Absolute zero means frozen' — the correct classical interpretation is K=0 initially but energy can still be transferred by heating.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims absolute zero is a permanent constraint preventing any subsequent motion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Establishes the initial condition; absorbs the pitfall of claiming the particle stays permanently frozen.

items.title: Motion is not diffusion
items.description: Explicitly states the particle's motion cannot be considered diffusion, nor partially diffusive, regardless of whether the trajectory appears random or spreading.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Ballistic mistaken for diffusion' — heating sounds like thermal random motion, but the single particle in vacuum undergoes ballistic motion, not diffusion.
provenance.discriminates: A response that concludes the motion is diffusion due to apparent randomness from thermal contact.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly answers whether the motion is diffusion; central to the question.

items.title: Diffusion requires interaction
items.description: States diffusion requires interaction with other particles in a medium, specifically many-body random collisions with a short mean free path, which a single particle in vacuum lacks.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts and the reference agree: diffusion requires many-body collisions in a surrounding medium, which the single particle in vacuum lacks.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says diffusion is possible for an isolated particle or omits the requirement of other particles.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Provides the physical reason the motion is not diffusion; the core explanatory claim.

items.title: Vacuum lacks medium
items.description: Identifies the vacuum tube as lacking a surrounding medium for particle collisions, which is why diffusive behavior cannot arise.

provenance.evidence_detail: Implicit constraint: the vacuum tube means no surrounding gas to provide random collisions needed for diffusion.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats the vacuum as irrelevant or equivalent to a gas-filled container.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects the vacuum condition to the absence of diffusion; supporting reasoning.

items.title: Temperature is statistical
items.description: States temperature is a statistical concept applicable to collections of particles rather than to a single particle.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (c) asks to discuss the concept of temperature and its applicability to single particles versus collections; all correct rollouts identify temperature as ensemble-defined.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats temperature as an intrinsic property of any individual particle.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly addresses the requested discussion of the concept of temperature and its applicability.

items.title: Single particle lacks temperature
items.description: States a single particle does not possess a well-defined thermodynamic temperature.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among all correct rollouts: a single particle has definite kinetic energy but no well-defined thermodynamic temperature.
provenance.discriminates: A response that assigns a thermodynamic temperature to the lone particle without qualification.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Applies the statistical nature of temperature to this specific single-particle scenario.

items.title: KE without temperature
items.description: States the single particle has a definite kinetic energy but not a thermodynamic temperature, distinguishing the two concepts.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus claim: single particle has definite kinetic energy but no well-defined thermodynamic temperature; only an effective temperature via reservoir equilibration.
provenance.discriminates: A response that conflates kinetic energy with temperature for one particle.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key distinction between mechanical energy and thermodynamic temperature for a single particle.

items.title: Temperature via reservoir
items.description: States that assigning a temperature to a single particle requires equilibration with a reservoir, providing the condition under which the notion becomes.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus claim among correct rollouts: only an effective temperature can be inferred if the particle equilibrates with a reservoir.
provenance.discriminates: A response that denies any temperature-related concept can apply to a single particle even in reservoir contact.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds depth on when a single-particle temperature could be defined; beyond the core answer.

items.title: Ballistic motion in vacuum
items.description: Describes the particle motion as ballistic in the vacuum between collisions with walls or the metal tray, rather than as a random walk.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among correct rollouts: straight-line ballistic trajectories between collisions with tray or walls; no gas medium for random collisions.
provenance.discriminates: A response that describes the motion as a random walk or Brownian motion in the vacuum.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct physical description of single-particle motion in vacuum; distinguishes from diffusive motion.

items.title: Avoids equipartition temperature
items.description: Avoids applying the equipartition relation to assign an intrinsic thermodynamic temperature to the single particle.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Temperature assigned to one particle' — directly applying ⟨E_k⟩ = (3/2)k_BT to one particle and treating the result as its thermodynamic temperature ignores the ensemble requirement.
provenance.discriminates: A response that computes T from one particle's kinetic energy using equipartition and calls it the particle's temperature.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific formula-level error that gives a false temperature for a single particle.

items.title: Avoids frozen-at-zero claim
items.description: Avoids claiming the particle remains permanently at rest because it started at absolute zero, since heating the tray adds energy to the particle.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Absolute zero means frozen' — absolute zero is an initial condition, not a permanent constraint; heating the tray transfers energy to the particle.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says the particle can never move because it began at absolute zero.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific wrong conclusion that ignores the effect of subsequent heating.

items.title: Avoids MSD formula trap
items.description: Avoids citing the mean-squared-displacement diffusion formula as evidence that the single particle's motion is diffusion.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'MSD formula dimension mismatch' — quoting ⟨Δr²⟩ ∝ t to justify diffusion is misleading because the motion is ballistic with ⟨Δr²⟩ ∝ t² in vacuum.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes down the MSD diffusion formula and uses it to argue the motion is or resembles diffusion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific formula-level error that misclassifies ballistic motion as diffusive using an inapplicable relation.

items.title: Diffusion needs other particles
items.description: States diffusion requires interaction with other particles in a medium.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts and the reference agree: diffusion requires many-body collisions in a surrounding medium, which the single particle in vacuum lacks.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says diffusion is possible for an isolated particle or omits the requirement of other particles.

items.title: Unit modulus of det U
items.description: States that |det U|^2 = 1 for a unitary matrix, equivalently that the determinant has unit modulus.

provenance.evidence_detail: Part (a) asks for the determinant of a general unitary matrix; the reference gives |det U|^2 = 1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states det U = 0, det U = ±1 only, or gives no modulus constraint.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core result for part 1; correctness collapses without it.

items.title: Phase form of det U
items.description: States det U = e^{iα} where α is a real number, giving the complex phase form of the determinant.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference states det U = e^{iα} with α real; all rollouts agreed.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes det U = ±1 (losing the general phase) or omits the e^{iα} form.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explicit answer to the first sub-question; directly required.

items.title: Starting identity det(UU†)=1
items.description: Uses det(UU†) = det(I) = 1 as the starting identity to derive the unit-modulus property of the determinant.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts and the reference begin from U†U = I, taking det of both sides.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts |det U| = 1 without any derivation or starting identity.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key derivation step; load-bearing intermediate for the proof.

items.title: det(U†) conjugate relation
items.description: States det(U†) = (det U)*, i.e., the determinant of the adjoint is the complex conjugate of the determinant.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'det(U†) not conjugated' warns against writing det(U†) = det(U), which forces det U = ±1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes det(U†) = det(U) without conjugation, which would wrongly restrict det U to ±1.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate to connect det(UU†) to |det U|^2.

items.title: det(exp(iF)) identity
items.description: States det(exp(iF̂)) = exp(i Tr F̂) as the explicit determinant of the operator Û = exp(iF̂).

provenance.evidence_detail: Part (b) asks to calculate det explicitly; reference gives det U = exp(i Tr F).
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives det[exp(iF)] = Tr(exp(iF)), det = exp(Tr F) without the i, or no explicit formula.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core requested quantity for part 2; correctness collapses without it.

items.title: Eigenvalue derivation of det
items.description: Diagonalizes F̂ = V diag(f_k) V†, shows eigenvalues of exp(iF̂) are e^{if_k}, and takes the product ∏ e^{if_k} = exp(i Σ f_k) = exp(i Tr F̂).

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Spectrum not used' warns against citing the trace identity without deriving via the spectral theorem.
provenance.discriminates: A response that quotes det(exp(A)) = exp(Tr A) without showing the diagonalization or spectrum connection.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explicit derivation from known spectrum; connects eigenvalues to trace formula.

items.title: Trace equals eigenvalue sum
items.description: Identifies Tr F̂ = Σ_k f_k, connecting the trace of F̂ to the sum of its eigenvalues from the known spectrum.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts used Tr F = Σ f_k as the link between eigenvalues and the trace formula.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes exp(i Tr F) without explicitly stating that Tr F equals the sum of eigenvalues f_k.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth; links trace to spectrum explicitly.

items.title: Scalar c and transformed U'
items.description: States c = (det U)^{-1/N} = e^{-iα/N} where N is the rank, and writes the transform U' = cU explicitly.

provenance.evidence_detail: Divergence between reference (c = e^{iα/N}) and mathematically correct c = e^{-iα/N}; rollouts all used the correct negative sign.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes c = e^{+iα/N} (the reference's sign error), which gives det(cU) = e^{2iα} ≠ 1.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core requested result for part 3; the specific scalar is load-bearing.

items.title: det(cU) scaling rule
items.description: States det(cU) = c^N det U for an N×N matrix, including the factor of N from the rank.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts correctly used det(cU) = c^N det U; mined pitfall 'Missing factor N' warns against det(cU) = c·det(U).
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes det(cU) = c·det(U), losing the factor N and yielding c = (det U)^{-1} instead of (det U)^{-1/N}.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key intermediate step to verify det U' = 1; rank factor is essential.

items.title: Verification det U' = 1
items.description: Substitutes to show c^N det U = e^{-iα}·e^{iα} = 1, confirming det U' = 1 for the transform.

provenance.evidence_detail: Part (c) requires proving det U' = 1; the verification step is the core of the proof.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts det U' = 1 without showing the substitution c^N det U = 1.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Completes the proof for the third sub-question; verifies unimodularity.

items.title: Existence proof for c
items.description: Proves c always exists because det U = e^{iα} ≠ 0, so (det U)^{-1/N} is well-defined.

provenance.evidence_detail: Part (c) explicitly asks to prove existence of such a transform; the nonzero determinant guarantees c is defined.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives c without justifying why it always exists, i.e., without noting det U ≠ 0.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Answer to 'prove there always exists'; correctness collapses without it.

items.title: Hermiticity gives real eigenvalues
items.description: Uses the hermiticity of F̂ to state its eigenvalues f_k are real, confirming |e^{if_k}| = 1 and linking F̂ to the unitary property.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Hermiticity of F unused' warns that the reality of eigenvalues is what ensures unitarity of exp(iF).
provenance.discriminates: A response that computes det[exp(iF)] without ever invoking that F Hermitian implies f_k real and |e^{if_k}| = 1.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth; connects hermiticity to unitarity of exp(iF̂).

items.title: Unitary eigenvalues unit modulus
items.description: States that eigenvalues u_k of a unitary matrix have |u_k| = 1, providing an alternative argument for |det U| = 1.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference mentions 'the same result follows from the property of eigenvalues' of the unitary matrix.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses only the det(UU†) argument without noting the eigenvalue property of unitary matrices.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Supplementary alternative derivation; minor added value.

items.title: General det(exp A) identity
items.description: States the general matrix identity det(exp(A)) = exp(Tr(A)) for any square matrix A, as the underlying identity used in the calculation.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference cites 'according to Problem 1.52' the identity det U = exp(i Tr F); rollouts derived it from scratch.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives det[exp(iF)] = exp(i Tr F) only for this specific case without stating or identifying the general identity.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth; generalizes the specific identity to arbitrary matrices.

items.title: Hermiticity implies unitarity
items.description: Shows Û = exp(iF̂) is unitary because F̂ hermitian implies (exp(iF̂))† = exp(-iF̂), so their product is the identity matrix.

provenance.evidence_detail: Related to mined pitfall 'Hermiticity of F unused'; the question defines U = exp(iF) without explicitly stating it is unitary.
provenance.discriminates: A response that takes U = exp(iF) as unitary without showing F Hermitian implies (exp(iF))† = exp(-iF).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth; justifies why Û = exp(iF̂) is unitary in the first place.

items.title: Product structure correct
items.description: The response identifies the product as CH3COCH2CH(CH3)2 (4-methylpentan-2-one), recognizing the implicit hydrogen on the carbon bearing two methyl groups to give a 6-carbon methyl ketone.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts correctly identified the implicit H in the C(CH3)2 notation; this is the central structural resolution of the problem.
provenance.discriminates: A response that reads CH3COCH2C(CH3)2 literally as a quaternary carbon with no hydrogen and attempts an impossible or 7-carbon synthesis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core correctness; misreading the product structure invalidates the entire synthesis.

items.title: Starting materials identified
items.description: The response shows acetylene (HC≡CH, 2 carbon atoms) and 2-methylpropane ((CH3)3CH, 4 carbon atoms) as the two starting materials.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question a requires drawing the target product and the two given starting materials.
provenance.discriminates: A response that misidentifies the starting materials or their carbon counts.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Foundational; without correct starting materials no synthesis can be correct.

items.title: Acetylide alkylation strategy
items.description: The response identifies acetylide alkylation as the carbon-carbon bond-forming step, using NaNH2 to deprotonate acetylene followed by alkylation with a primary alkyl halide.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question b asks for identification of the C–C bond-forming strategy via acetylide alkylation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that proposes a different bond-forming strategy or does not specify the acetylide SN2 mechanism.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning step; only C–C bond method available at this stage of the course.

items.title: Terminal alkyne intermediate
items.description: The response shows the 6-carbon terminal alkyne intermediate HC≡C–CH2CH(CH3)2 formed from acetylide alkylation of acetylene with isobutyl bromide.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question c requires drawing the terminal alkyne intermediate obtained after NaNH2 treatment and alkylation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that draws an internal alkyne, an alkyne with wrong connectivity, or fails to show this intermediate.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Critical intermediate linking the two starting material fragments.

items.title: Hydration gives methyl ketone
items.description: The response states that acid-catalyzed hydration of the terminal alkyne with H2SO4, H2O, and HgSO4 produces the methyl ketone CH3COCH2CH(CH3)2 with the carbonyl on the internal carbon.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Markovnikov hydration reversal' (medium severity): confusing the regiochemistry with hydroboration-oxidation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that draws an aldehyde rather than the methyl ketone from the H2SO4/H2O/HgSO4 hydration.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Final step producing the target; wrong regiochemistry gives aldehyde, not ketone.

items.title: Radical bromination tertiary
items.description: The response shows that radical bromination of 2-methylpropane with Br2/hv selectively gives the tertiary alkyl bromide (CH3)3CBr because bromine radicals preferentially abstract the tertiary C–H bond.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Radical bromination selectivity' (medium severity): assuming primary bromide is obtained directly.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states Br2/hv on 2-methylpropane gives (CH3)2CHCH2Br directly.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Selectivity is load-bearing; claiming direct primary bromide skips required steps.

items.title: E2 elimination to 2-methylpropene
items.description: The response shows that treatment of the tertiary bromide (CH3)3CBr with NaOEt produces 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, via E2 elimination rather than substitution.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Elimination vs substitution' (low severity): NaOEt can give SN1/E1 competition with a tertiary substrate.
provenance.discriminates: A response that shows an ether product from the NaOEt step rather than the alkene.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate; substitution would produce ether and block synthesis.

items.title: Anti-Markovnikov HBr addition
items.description: The response shows that addition of HBr/ROOR to 2-methylpropene gives the primary isobutyl bromide (CH3)2CHCH2Br via anti-Markovnikov addition, not Markovnikov addition which would reform the tertiary bromide.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'HBr without peroxide' (high severity): omitting ROOR reverses the regiochemistry and defeats the relocation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that specifies plain HBr without ROOR for the alkene-to-primary-bromide step.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Produces the required primary halide; without peroxide the wrong regioisomer forms.

items.title: SN2 requires primary halide
items.description: The response explains that the tertiary bromide (CH3)3CBr cannot undergo SN2 alkylation with acetylide and therefore must be converted to the primary isobutyl bromide before the alkylation step.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Tertiary halide in SN2' (high severity): skipping the relocation sequence and attempting SN2 at a tertiary carbon.
provenance.discriminates: A response that directly alkylates the acetylide with the tertiary bromide, skipping the NaOEt elimination and HBr/ROOR steps.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key mechanistic reasoning justifying the extra steps; directly addresses the disputed point.

items.title: Complete synthesis in order
items.description: The response presents the entire synthesis in correct order: Br2/hv on 2-methylpropane, then NaOEt elimination, then HBr/ROOR, then NaNH2/alkylation of acetylene, then H2SO4/H2O/HgSO4 hydration.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question h requires the complete synthesis scheme with all reagents and intermediates.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits steps, reagents, or intermediates from the final synthesis summary.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Integrative; correct ordering of all steps is essential for a valid synthesis route.

items.title: Mono-alkylation of acetylene
items.description: The response uses one equivalent of NaNH2 to generate the mono-acetylide ion HC≡C⁻, which undergoes a single alkylation with the primary alkyl halide to give the terminal alkyne rather than a dialkylated internal alkyne.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Double deprotonation of acetylene' warns against over-alkylation; one equivalent gives the desired terminal alkyne.
provenance.discriminates: A response that shows dialkylation of acetylene to give an internal alkyne instead of the terminal alkyne intermediate.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Prevents over-alkylation; important for obtaining the correct terminal alkyne intermediate.

items.title: Carbon count verification
items.description: The response confirms that the 2-carbon acetylene fragment plus the 4-carbon 2-methylpropane fragment combine to give the 6-carbon product via one new carbon-carbon bond.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts validated the carbon count: 2C + 4C = 6C via a single C–C bond formation.
provenance.discriminates: A response whose intermediates or product do not conserve carbon count at 6 atoms total.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Useful sanity check but not mechanistically load-bearing on its own.

items.title: Avoids quaternary carbon misread
items.description: Avoids interpreting the product notation CH3COCH2C(CH3)2 literally as a quaternary carbon with no hydrogen, instead recognizing the implicit H to give CH3COCH2CH(CH3)2.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Missing H in product' (high severity): literal reading of C(CH3)2 as quaternary gives wrong carbon count and connectivity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats the product as having a quaternary carbon and designs a synthesis for a different or impossible structure.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific misreading observed; correcting it changes the entire target structure.

items.title: Avoids wrong hydration regiochemistry
items.description: Avoids placing the carbonyl at the terminal carbon during HgSO4-catalyzed hydration, which would produce an aldehyde instead of the desired methyl ketone.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Markovnikov hydration reversal' (medium severity): confusing the regiochemistry with hydroboration-oxidation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that draws an aldehyde rather than the methyl ketone from the H2SO4/H2O/HgSO4 hydration.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Classic regiochemistry trap; wrong placement gives a different functional group.

items.title: Avoids substitution over elimination
items.description: Avoids using conditions that favor substitution over elimination when treating the tertiary bromide with NaOEt, which would produce tert-butyl ethyl ether instead of 2-methylpropene.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Elimination vs substitution' (low severity): NaOEt can give SN1/E1 competition with a tertiary substrate.
provenance.discriminates: A response that shows an ether product from the NaOEt step rather than the alkene.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Tertiary substrates can undergo SN1; specifying E2 conditions is the real distinction.

items.title: Contradiction assumption
items.description: The response sets up a proof by contradiction by assuming, in search of a contradiction, that μ_k is larger than μ_s.

provenance.evidence_detail: The target is a physical justification that μ_s ≥ μ_k; the reference uses contradiction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that merely asserts the inequality without any logical argument.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core logical structure; without it the argument collapses. Directly addresses the sub-question.

items.title: Problematic force range
items.description: The response identifies the applied force range μ_s N < F < μ_k N as the region where the contradiction arises.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollouts 1 and 2 matched the reference by giving the full range; Rollout 3 only tested the single threshold point.
provenance.discriminates: A response that only checks F = μ_s N instead of the full interval between the two thresholds.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Pinpoints where both moving and not-moving conclusions clash; key intermediate reasoning step.

items.title: Force below μ_s N
items.description: The response states that for an applied force smaller than μ_s N, static friction exactly cancels it using f_{s,max} = μ_s N, so the block does not move.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts agreed on this formula.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a wrong expression for the static threshold.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Establishes baseline behavior below threshold; required intermediate for the contradiction argument.

items.title: Force exceeds μ_s N
items.description: The response states that when the applied force exceeds μ_s N, which is the maximum static friction force by definition, the block should move.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly states the applied force exceeds μ_s N so the block should move.
provenance.discriminates: A response that does not establish the first half of the contradiction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: One horn of the contradiction; essential to showing why the problematic range is contradictory.

items.title: Kinetic friction stops block
items.description: The response states that once the block moves even the slightest infinitesimal amount, kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N becomes the relevant force and, being larger than the applied force, decelerates the block back to rest.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts agreed on this formula.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a wrong expression for kinetic friction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The other horn of the contradiction; explains why motion is impossible in the problematic range.

items.title: No motion for point B
items.description: The response concludes the block actually never moves at all for the applied force represented by point B in the problematic range, because kinetic friction wins out over the applied force.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states the block never moves even for the force represented by point B.
provenance.discriminates: A response that leaves the motion status ambiguous.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Synthesis step leading to the contradiction; bridges the two horns into the final conclusion.

items.title: Final inequality μ_s ≥ μ_k
items.description: The response concludes that the contradiction arises unless μ_s N ≥ μ_k N, so it must be the case that μ_s ≥ μ_k, and there then exists no point B below μ_k N and above μ_s N.

provenance.evidence_detail: The target of the question is the inequality μ_s ≥ μ_k.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gets the inequality direction wrong or omits the conclusion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The answer's final result; without it the response does not answer the question.

items.title: Avoids static persists sliding
items.description: Avoids claiming that static friction adjusts up to the larger μ_k N value and still applies once the block begins to slide.

provenance.evidence_detail: The high-severity wrong-friction-regime pitfall.
provenance.discriminates: A response that erases the contradiction by treating μ_k N as a static threshold.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common conceptual error observed; conflates which friction regime governs a sliding block.

items.title: Avoids bare assertion
items.description: Avoids stating μ_s ≥ μ_k as an empirical fact without giving the logical contradiction that forces the inequality.

provenance.evidence_detail: The medium-severity bare-assertion-no-proof pitfall.
provenance.discriminates: A response that only cites asperity interlocking as the reason and skips the proof.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Question asks 'why'; bare assertion misses the entire requested derivation.

items.title: Microscopic asperity view
items.description: The response explains that microscopic asperities interlock when the block rests on the surface and are continuously broken or reformed during sliding, making static contacts stronger than sliding contacts.

provenance.evidence_detail: Correct rollouts included the microscopic explanation as supporting intuition.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives only formal logic with no physical mechanism.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added physical depth beyond the logical argument; not required for correctness.

items.title: Maximum static friction formula
items.description: The response uses the formula f_{s,max} = μ_s N for the maximum static friction force.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts agreed on this formula.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a wrong expression for the static threshold.
