items.title: Core condition stated
items.description: The response states that the zero potential level is an excited state if there exists at least one state with negative potential energy (E < 0).

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) requires the precise condition; the reference answer gives this as its sole content.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives a vague or incorrect condition, or never states the existence-of-negative-energy-state requirement.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly answers the question; highest-importance anchor with no duplicates.

items.title: Ground state defined
items.description: The response defines the ground state as the eigenstate with the lowest energy in the quantum system.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) requires justifying the condition by reference to the definition of excited states, which depends on the ground-state definition.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states the condition but never defines the ground state as the lowest-energy eigenstate.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Load-bearing definition for the logical argument; no measured discrimination but structurally required.

items.title: Excited state defined
items.description: The response defines an excited state as any energy eigenstate whose energy lies above the ground-state energy, so E = 0 is excited exactly when the ground state has energy below zero.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Stopping at condition, skipping justification' (severity: medium): giving the bare condition without the definitional link.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states the condition but never connects it to the definition of excited states.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Definition directly justifies the condition; merged duplicate sharpens the link to E=0.

items.title: Logical link to E=0
items.description: The response explicitly connects the definition to the conclusion: if a negative-energy eigenstate exists, the ground state has E_gs < 0, so E = 0 lies above the ground state and is excited.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) requires the justification linking the condition to the excited-state definition.
provenance.discriminates: A response that lists both the condition and the definition separately but never connects them.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Bridges definition to conclusion; central reasoning step in the justification.

items.title: Negative energy lowers ground
items.description: The response states that the existence of states with negative potential energy implies the ground state energy is below zero (E_gs < 0), so the zero level cannot be the ground state.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct item: 'Role of negative-energy states' — if negative eigenstates exist, the ground state lies below zero.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions negative-energy states but does not identify their consequence for the ground-state energy value.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Merged duplicate; key implication that makes E=0 excited, directly supports core answer.

items.title: E=0 eigenvalue requirement
items.description: The response notes that for the zero potential level to be classified as an excited state, E = 0 must correspond to an actual energy eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian, not merely an arbitrary reference point.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct item: 'E=0 must be an actual eigenstate' — all three rollouts noted this requirement.
provenance.discriminates: A response that classifies E=0 as excited without requiring it to be a genuine Hamiltonian eigenvalue.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Merged duplicate; structural qualifier that prevents overclaim, important for correctness.

items.title: Relative ordering of eigenvalues
items.description: The response explains that the set of allowed energy eigenvalues and their relative ordering determine which state is the ground state and which are excited, not the absolute value of any single energy level.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (c) asks to explain the role of potential levels in defining excited versus ground states.
provenance.discriminates: A response that never discusses how the energy eigenvalue spectrum and its ordering classify states.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Merged triplicate; real depth but not load-bearing for the core condition.

items.title: Role of potential levels
items.description: The response includes a discussion of the role of potential levels in determining the energy spectrum of the quantum system and the classification of states as ground or excited.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Unanswered sub-question on role' (severity: low): leaving sub-question (c) silently unanswered.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers the condition and justification but omits any discussion of the role of potential levels.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Question explicitly requests role of potential levels; covers a required sub-question.

items.title: Avoids reversed ordering
items.description: Avoids stating that E = 0 is the ground state and that negative-energy states are excited relative to zero, which reverses the definition of the ground state as the lowest-energy eigenstate.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Reversed ordering of ground state' (severity: high): reasoning that negative-energy states make zero the ground state.
provenance.discriminates: A response that concludes the zero level is the ground state when negative-energy states exist.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific observed error that inverts the entire argument; high discriminative potential.

items.title: Avoids arbitrariness dismissal
items.description: Avoids concluding that the zero potential level can never be classified as excited merely because the zero of potential energy is an arbitrary reference choice.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Arbitrary reference no-conclusion' (severity: high): arguing the question is meaningless because potential zero is arbitrary.
provenance.discriminates: A response that dismisses the entire question by invoking the arbitrariness of the potential zero.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Observed dismissal pattern; pitfall unique to this question's disputed point.

items.title: Avoids convention-as-ground
items.description: Avoids assuming that the ground state energy is always defined to be zero by convention, which would make E = 0 automatically the ground state and never excited.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Ground state = zero by convention' (severity: medium): assuming E_gs is always renormalized to zero.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims the zero level is always the ground state because ground-state energy is defined as zero.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific observed misconception; directly undermines the core condition.

items.title: Arbitrariness acknowledged
items.description: The response acknowledges that the zero of potential energy is an arbitrary reference choice but notes that once a reference is fixed, the relative ordering of eigenvalues has physical implications.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct item: 'Zero of potential is arbitrary' — adding a constant C shifts all eigenvalues without changing ground/excited classification.
provenance.discriminates: A response that either ignores the arbitrariness entirely or uses it to dismiss the question.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses the disputed point with real depth; optional but adds precision.

items.title: Shift invariance noted
items.description: The response states that adding a constant to the potential shifts all energy eigenvalues by the same constant without changing which state is the ground state and which are excited.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct item: 'Zero of potential is arbitrary' — the shift invariance of classification.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims shifting the potential changes which state is ground or excited.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Genuine physics insight but tangential to the core condition; low weight.

items.title: Continuum caveat
items.description: The response acknowledges that if E = 0 lies at a continuum threshold rather than being a discrete eigenvalue, the zero level may not be a normalizable excited bound state.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Ignoring continuum/threshold caveat' (severity: medium) and divergence on whether E=0 must be discrete.
provenance.discriminates: A response that unqualifiedly asserts E=0 is always a discrete excited eigenstate whenever negative bound states exist.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Advanced edge case; real but minor depth, not required for the core answer.

items.title: Negative states lower ground
items.description: The response states that if negative-energy eigenstates exist, the ground state energy E_gs is negative (E_gs < 0).

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct item: 'Role of negative-energy states' — if negative eigenstates exist, the ground state lies below zero.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions negative-energy states but does not identify their consequence for the ground-state energy value.

items.title: Option (a) selected
items.description: States that option (a), d_A < d_F, is a necessary condition for the equilibrium of the connected spheres.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) asks whether d_A < d_F is necessary; the reference answer confirms it is correct.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits or rejects option (a) misses the condition required for the lighter sphere to need a downward tension.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct final option; essential to the answer, no discrimination data but core requirement.

items.title: Option (b) selected
items.description: States that option (b), d_B > d_F, is a necessary condition for the equilibrium of the connected spheres.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) asks whether d_B > d_F is necessary; the reference answer confirms it is correct.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits or rejects option (b) misses the condition required for the denser sphere to need an upward tension.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct final option; essential to the answer, no discrimination data but core requirement.

items.title: Option (d) selected
items.description: States that option (d), d_A + d_B = 2d_F, is a necessary condition for the equilibrium of the connected spheres.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (d) asks whether d_A + d_B = 2d_F is necessary; the reference answer confirms it is correct.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits option (d) has not equated the two tension expressions and misses the average-density constraint.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct final option; essential to the answer, no discrimination data but core requirement.

items.title: Avoids option (c)
items.description: Avoids selecting option (c), d_A > d_F, as a valid condition for the equilibrium of the connected spheres.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (c) asks whether d_A > d_F is necessary; the reference answer does not list it among the correct options.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects option (c) has reversed the tension direction or misidentified which sphere must be lighter than the fluid.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific trap: (c) contradicts (a); observed confusion justifies moderate pitfall weight.

items.title: Force balance sphere A
items.description: Writes the force balance for sphere A immersed in the fluid as d_F V g upward equals d_A V g downward plus tension T downward.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts wrote this per-sphere equation for sphere A; the system-only pitfall demonstrates it is load-bearing.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes only the combined-system equation cannot derive the individual density inequalities.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key intermediate equation; load-bearing for deriving tension and density conditions.
provenance.merged_mirror_text: Writes the force balance for sphere B immersed in the fluid as d_F V g upward plus tension T upward equals d_B V g downward.

items.title: Tension expression A
items.description: Derives the tension in the string on sphere A as T = (d_F − d_A) V g from the force balance.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus rollouts all derived this expression; the reversed-tension pitfall yields the wrong sign (d_A − d_F) instead.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes T = (d_A − d_F)Vg has reversed the tension direction and would select option (c).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate result connecting force balance to the density inequality for sphere A.
provenance.merged_mirror_text: Derives the tension in the string on sphere B as T = (d_B − d_F) V g from the force balance.

items.title: Equate tensions
items.description: Sets the two tension expressions for the connected spheres equal, (d_F − d_A)Vg = (d_B − d_F)Vg, to derive d_A + d_B = 2d_F.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts performed this step; the not-equating-tensions pitfall shows omitting it drops option (d).
provenance.discriminates: A response that derives (a) and (b) but never equates the two T expressions will miss option (d).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key algebraic step yielding option (d); central derivation link in the solution.

items.title: T strictly positive
items.description: States that the tension T in the string is strictly positive (T > 0) because the arrangement has a taut string with nonzero tension.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts imposed T > 0; the dropping-T>0 pitfall shows that without it only option (d) survives.
provenance.discriminates: A response that allows T = 0 would accept d_A = d_F or d_B = d_F and fail to obtain the strict inequalities in options (a) and (b).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Necessary physical assumption enabling both density inequalities; bridges tensions to options (a) and (b).

items.title: Derive d_A < d_F
items.description: Derives d_A < d_F from the condition that the tension expression T = (d_F − d_A)Vg is strictly positive for immersed sphere A.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts connected T > 0 on sphere A to the inequality d_A < d_F; the dropping-T>0 pitfall targets this step.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states d_A < d_F as a guess without connecting it to T > 0 has not completed the required justification.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Direct derivation of option (a); important step but follows from prior tension result.
provenance.merged_mirror_text: Derives d_B > d_F from the condition that the tension expression T = (d_B − d_F)Vg is strictly positive for immersed sphere B.

items.title: Buoyant force formula
items.description: States that the buoyant force on each fully immersed sphere has magnitude d_F times V times g directed upward.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts used the buoyant force formula d_F·V·g; it is a load-bearing intermediate quantity for the force balances.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a wrong buoyant force magnitude (e.g., d_A·V·g) would produce incorrect tension expressions.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Basic supporting formula; adds depth but force balance items already subsume it.

items.title: Weight formulas
items.description: States the weights of the two solid spheres as d_A times V times g and d_B times V times g respectively.

provenance.evidence_detail: All consensus rollouts wrote the weight expressions; they are load-bearing intermediate quantities.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses mass instead of density times volume in the weight would not derive the density-based conditions.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Basic supporting formula; adds depth but force balance items already subsume it.

items.title: Average density insight
items.description: States that the relation d_A + d_B = 2d_F means the average density of the two solid spheres equals the fluid density d_F.

provenance.calibration_rationale: Conceptual insight enriching option (d); real but non-essential added depth.

items.title: States starting equation
items.description: States the equation PV = nRT as the starting point of the derivation.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question explicitly asks to begin from PV = nRT; all rollouts and the reference do so.
provenance.discriminates: A response that jumps to a final formula without anchoring it to the ideal gas equation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Foundational equation; without it the derivation cannot begin.

items.title: Substitutes n correctly
items.description: Substitutes n equal to mass divided by molar mass into the equation PV = nRT and writes the substituted form PV equals mass times RT divided by molar mass.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Number density for mass density' pitfall identifies failure to introduce molar mass via n = mass/molar mass as the critical missing step.
provenance.discriminates: A response that rearranges PV = nRT to n/V = P/(RT) and calls that 'density' without ever substituting n = mass/molar mass.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key substitution linking moles to mass; absorbs the n = mass×molar mass pitfall.

items.title: Isolates mass over volume
items.description: Rearranges the equation to isolate mass divided by volume on one side.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference shows the step w/V = Pm/(RT); all rollouts produce the equivalent m/V = PM/(RT).
provenance.discriminates: A response that substitutes n = m/M but leaves the equation in the form PV = (m/M)RT without isolating the density term.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate step to connect the ideal gas equation to density.

items.title: Identifies density
items.description: Identifies mass per unit volume as density within the derivation.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Stopping one step early' pitfall notes that responses may rearrange correctly but never identify m/V as density.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes w/V = Pm/(RT) or m/V = PM/(RT) but never labels the left-hand side as density.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Bridges the algebraic rearrangement to the physical quantity density.

items.title: Arrives at density expression
items.description: Arrives at the expression density equals P times molar mass divided by RT, with pressure P and molar mass in the numerator and gas constant R and temperature T in the denominator.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Inverted algebra' pitfall places RT in the numerator instead of the denominator.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes density = P×M×RT or density = RT/(PM) instead of density = PM/(RT).
provenance.calibration_rationale: The central derived result; all flawed paths fail to reach this correct form.

items.title: Temperature held constant
items.description: Explicitly states that temperature is held constant when asserting the proportionality between density and pressure.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Missing constant-T justification' pitfall identifies responses that claim ρ ∝ P without invoking constant T.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes ρ = PM/(RT) and says ρ ∝ P but never mentions that temperature is fixed.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key constraint; proportionality breaks without constant temperature.

items.title: Molar mass constant for gas
items.description: States that molar mass is constant for a given gas, so the proportionality between density and pressure holds at a given temperature.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Missing constant-T justification' pitfall extends to noting that M, R, and T must all be constant for the proportionality to hold.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts ρ ∝ P without explaining why molar mass is a fixed quantity.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required assumption; without fixed molar mass the proportionality is invalid.

items.title: Concludes density ∝ P
items.description: Concludes that density is proportional to pressure at constant temperature for a given gas.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question's target is ρ ∝ P at fixed T; the reference and all rollouts state this explicitly.
provenance.discriminates: A response that derives the expression but never states the final proportionality between density and pressure.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The target result of the question; no correct answer omits this conclusion.

items.title: R is constant
items.description: References that the gas constant R is constant in the derivation leading to density being proportional to pressure.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Missing constant-T justification' pitfall notes that R must also be recognized as constant for the proportionality constant M/(RT) to be well-defined.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats R as a variable or never acknowledges it as a fixed constant.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds depth but is implicit in the use of the ideal gas equation.

items.title: Avoids number density
items.description: Avoids presenting n divided by V as the density result without substituting n equal to mass divided by molar mass into the equation PV = nRT.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Number density for mass density' pitfall (high severity) identifies the mistake of presenting n/V as density.
provenance.discriminates: A response that rearranges to n/V = P/(RT) and labels n/V as 'density' without ever introducing molar mass.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common error: reporting number density instead of mass density.

items.title: Avoids inverse proportionality
items.description: Avoids stating that density is proportional to 1 over P or inversely proportional to pressure, since density is proportional to pressure P at constant temperature.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Inverted algebra' pitfall (high severity) produces ρ ∝ 1/P instead of ρ ∝ P.
provenance.discriminates: A response that algebraically inverts the expression and concludes density decreases with increasing pressure.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly contradicts the target conclusion; high-impact mistake.

items.title: Avoids symbol collision
items.description: Avoids using the same symbol for sample mass and molar mass when substituting into the equation PV = nRT, so the density expression remains unambiguous.

provenance.evidence_detail: The 'Confusing mass and molar mass symbols' pitfall notes that both quantities are often denoted 'm', creating ambiguity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses 'm' for both mass and molar mass, making the substitution n = m/m ambiguous or dimensionally inconsistent.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Notation error that causes confusion in the derivation of density.

items.title: Pellet mass identified
items.description: The response identifies the mass of the pellets as 5.7 g.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference and all rollouts agree on mass = 5.7 g as a load-bearing input.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a different mass value or omits it entirely.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core input value; without it the entire calculation fails.

items.title: Displaced volume computed
items.description: The response computes the volume of water displaced by the pellets as 7.7 ml − 5.0 ml = 2.7 ml.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts and the reference agree the displaced volume is 2.7 ml; this is the core displacement step.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses 7.7 ml, 5.0 ml, or a sum as the pellet volume.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key intermediate step; errors here propagate to every downstream result.

items.title: Density formula applied
items.description: The response applies the density formula as mass divided by volume using 5.7 g / 2.7 ml.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer shows ρ = 5.7 g / 2.7 ml as the load-bearing ratio.
provenance.discriminates: A response that inverts the ratio to 2.7 / 5.7 or uses wrong operands.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Load-bearing formula; incorrect setup yields wrong density.

items.title: Final density value
items.description: The response reports the density of the pellets as 2.1 g/ml.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Reporting volume not density' (medium severity) predicts stopping at 2.7 ml.
provenance.discriminates: A response whose final answer is 2.7 ml rather than 2.1 g/ml.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly answers the question; absorbs the pitfall of reporting 2.7 ml instead.

items.title: Correct density units
items.description: The response attaches the units g/ml to the reported density value.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Missing or wrong units' identifies omitting or mislabeling units as a failure mode.
provenance.discriminates: A response that reports 2.1 with no units or with units such as g or ml.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Units distinguish density from a bare number; adds correctness but is secondary.

items.title: Displacement rationale
items.description: The response states that the volume of the pellets equals the volume of water displaced, referencing the graduated cylinder water level readings.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly identifies the pellet volume as the volume of water displaced.
provenance.discriminates: A response that computes the right number without connecting it to the displacement principle.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Conceptual justification for the subtraction step; deepens correctness.

items.title: Avoids wrong volume
items.description: Avoids using an incorrect pellet volume such as 7.7 ml alone, 5.0 ml alone, or 12.7 ml from adding the two readings instead of subtracting.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Final volume as pellet volume' (high severity) predicts using 7.7 ml as the volume, yielding 0.74 g/ml.
provenance.discriminates: A response that computes 5.7 / 7.7 and reports approximately 0.74 g/ml.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Names three specific observed wrong-volume methods; high discriminative trap.

items.title: Avoids inverted ratio
items.description: Avoids dividing the displaced volume 2.7 ml by the mass 5.7 g to report approximately 0.47 as the density of the pellets.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Inverted density ratio' (high severity) predicts computing 2.7 / 5.7.
provenance.discriminates: A response that reports approximately 0.47 ml/g as the density of the pellets.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific inverted-ratio error observed in flawed responses; catches formula-direction mistakes.

items.title: Operational meaning of relativity
items.description: States that the empirical meaning of special relativity is operational, concerning observable instrument readings such as rods, clocks, and detectors, with no local experiment detecting absolute uniform motion.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) asks for a discussion of the empirical meaning of relativity; consensus among all rollouts was that SR is operational, not metaphysical.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives a purely philosophical or metaphysical account of relativity without grounding it in observable quantities.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core thesis of the question; anchors all operational SR discussion.

items.title: Spacetime interval invariance
items.description: States that the spacetime interval ds² = c²dt² − dx² − dy² − dz² is invariant under Lorentz transformations across different inertial frames in special relativity.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts agreed that spacetime interval invariance is a core SR principle.
provenance.discriminates: A response that discusses Lorentz transformations but never identifies the invariant quantity or gets its sign signature wrong.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Mathematical backbone of SR frame transformations; load-bearing formula.

items.title: Operational SR tests across frames
items.description: Describes at least one operational test of special relativity across different inertial frames, such as time dilation Δt = γΔτ, length contraction L = L₀/γ, or relativity of simultaneity Δt′ = −γvΔx/c².

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) explicitly asks how SR principles can be operationally tested when measuring events in different inertial frames.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names SR phenomena but never ties them to measurable procedures or correct transformation formulas.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly addresses the question's request for operational testing of SR.

items.title: Invariance of speed of light
items.description: States that the invariance of the speed of light c is an operationally tested principle of special relativity across different inertial frames.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts listed invariance of c among the operational tests of SR.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits the constancy of c, which is a defining postulate of SR that can be empirically tested.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Foundational SR principle; important but partially overlaps with item 2.

items.title: Position-momentum uncertainty
items.description: States that the Heisenberg uncertainty principle ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2 limits the spatial precision with which events can be localized in quantum mechanics.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (c) asks to address challenges posed by the uncertainty principle; all rollouts identified ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2 as limiting spatial localization.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions the uncertainty principle generically without specifying how it bounds event localization.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Central challenge posed by QM to event localization; directly requested.

items.title: Energy-time uncertainty
items.description: States that the energy-time uncertainty relation ΔEΔt ≥ ℏ/2 limits the temporal resolution of event measurement in quantum mechanics.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts identified ΔEΔt ≥ ℏ/2 as limiting temporal resolution of event measurement.
provenance.discriminates: A response that discusses spatial uncertainty only and ignores the temporal limitation on testing simultaneity or clock synchronization.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Complements position-momentum limit; addresses temporal aspect of SR testing.

items.title: Avoids misusing Δt notation
items.description: Avoids writing the energy-time uncertainty relation as ΔEΔt ~ ℏ/Δt with Δt appearing self-referentially on both sides, or presenting Δt as the standard deviation of a self-adjoint time operator with the same status as position-momentum uncertainty.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Circular Δt notation' (medium severity) observed in rollout 1's declared final answer.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes a dimensionally and logically inconsistent ΔEΔt expression from one that uses the correct form.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common conceptual error; merged two near-duplicate avoidance items.

items.title: Statistics bridges QM and SR
items.description: States that single quantum measurement outcomes are probabilistic, so statistics connects the limitations of measurement in quantum mechanics to the operational testing of special relativity, requiring statistical ensembles rather than individual deterministic events.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer emphasizes 'the role of statistics' as the unifying framework, whereas all rollouts treated statistics as one topic among several rather than the central connecting theme.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions probabilistic outcomes as a sub-topic rather than as the load-bearing bridge between QM measurement and SR covariance.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Reference answer emphasizes this bridge; high importance to the question.

items.title: Lorentz covariance of distributions
items.description: States that special relativity is tested in quantum mechanics by verifying the Lorentz covariance of probability distributions such as cross-sections, decay rates, and spectra across different frames, not by individual deterministic events.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed that SR in QM is tested via covariance of probability distributions across frames.
provenance.discriminates: A response that frames SR verification in terms of single-particle trajectory measurements without invoking distribution-level covariance.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Sharpest formulation of the QM-SR testing interface; names concrete observables.

items.title: Microcausality and no-signaling
items.description: States that spacelike-separated local observables commute, [O(x), O(y)] = 0 for (x−y)² < 0, ensuring no-signaling and Lorentz-covariant probability distributions in quantum mechanics.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed that no-signaling/microcausality ensures SR compatibility.
provenance.discriminates: A response that raises the challenge of frame-dependent measurement but never states the mechanism preserving Lorentz covariance.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Formal condition reconciling QM measurement with relativity; load-bearing.

items.title: Avoids collapse violating Lorentz
items.description: Avoids asserting or implying that wavefunction collapse is a physical process in a preferred frame that violates the principles of relativity or enables superluminal signaling between different inertial frames.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Collapse violates Lorentz' (high severity, foreseen) about claiming QM is incompatible with SR.
provenance.discriminates: A response that concludes QM measurement is fundamentally incompatible with SR from one that correctly treats collapse as a non-relativistic bookkeeping tool.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific misconception linking QM measurement collapse to SR violation.

items.title: Compton wavelength localization limit
items.description: States that below the Compton wavelength λ_C = ℏ/(mc), localization energy creates particle-antiparticle pairs, requiring quantum field theory rather than single-particle position operators.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts identified the Compton wavelength as the boundary where the single-particle picture breaks down.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts event positions can be localized to arbitrary precision in principle with only ΔxΔp as a bound.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Concrete physical bound on localization; deepens uncertainty discussion.

items.title: Avoids classical SR only
items.description: Avoids presenting special relativity as Lorentz transformations, time dilation, and length contraction without connecting them to the role of measurement, uncertainty, and statistics in quantum mechanics.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Classical SR only, QM grafted on' (high severity, reference_contrast) about not genuinely addressing QM measurement limits within SR operational tests.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats SR classically throughout and mentions the uncertainty principle only in a disconnected final paragraph.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Guards against ignoring half the question; observed common failure mode.

items.title: Energy-momentum relation as SR test
items.description: States that the relativistic energy-momentum relation E² = p²c² + m²c⁴ and its Lorentz transformation E′ = γ(E − vp_x), p′x = γ(p_x − vE/c²) are predictions of special relativity tested in different inertial frames.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollout 2 explicitly included the energy-momentum relation as an operational test; rollouts 1 and 3 did not; the reference is silent.
provenance.discriminates: A response that includes four-momentum covariance as an additional SR test from one that covers only spacetime coordinate transformations.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real but secondary SR test; adds depth without being central.

items.title: Photon position operator limitation
items.description: States that photons lack an exact position operator in quantum mechanics, complicating the localization of events involving photons in operational tests of relativity.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollout 2 explicitly stated photons lack an exact position operator; rollouts 1 and 3 did not; the reference is silent.
provenance.discriminates: A response that acknowledges the photon localization problem from one that assumes all particles including photons have well-defined position operators.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Genuine subtle limitation; optional depth on QM measurement challenges.

validation_summary.pitfall_weight_convention: stored on the RaR -1/-2 scale by schema.Criterion; graded by magnitude with polarity=positive

items.title: Selects Zn only
items.description: The response identifies exactly one option, (b) Zn, as the sole correct answer for this IIT-JEE 1980 question.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question asks which option dissolves; the reference answer shows Zn + 2NaOH reacting.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects (a), (c), (d), or no option.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without selecting Zn the response fails entirely.

items.title: Zn is amphoteric
items.description: The response states that Zn is the sole amphoteric metal among the options and therefore dissolves in hot concentrated NaOH.

provenance.evidence_detail: Amphoteric vs aqua-regia filter trap, severity high.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses broad 'dissolves in strong reagent' reasoning without checking amphoterism.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning that discriminates Zn from the other three metals.

items.title: Sodium zincate product
items.description: The response writes the reaction product as Na2ZnO2, naming it sodium zincate, in the equation Zn + 2NaOH → Na2ZnO2 + H2↑.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference uses Na2ZnO2; no rollout produced this exact formula.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes only Na2[Zn(OH)4] or omits the product formula.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Matches the reference answer exactly; canonical product for this reaction.

items.title: H2 evolution
items.description: The response includes H2↑ (hydrogen gas) as a product in the Zn + 2NaOH reaction equation.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts included H2, and the reference shows H2↑; the mined pitfall flags omission of H2.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes the equation without H2 as a product.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required product in the balanced equation; commonly omitted by flawed responses.

items.title: 2NaOH as reactant
items.description: The response writes the balanced reaction with 2NaOH as the reactant alongside Zn under heating (Δ).

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference equation specifies Zn + 2NaOH → Na2ZnO2 + H2↑.
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses an unbalanced or incorrect stoichiometric coefficient for NaOH.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct stoichiometry; load-bearing for the balanced equation.

items.title: Rejects Fe
items.description: The response states or implies that option (a) Fe does not dissolve in hot concentrated NaOH because Fe hydroxides are basic.

provenance.evidence_detail: Fe acid-base confusion trap, severity medium.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects (a) Fe because Fe reacts with acids or appears in chlor-alkali contexts.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Eliminates a common distractor; reinforces amphoteric reasoning.

items.title: Rejects Cu
items.description: The response states or implies that option (c) Cu does not dissolve in hot concentrated NaOH, noting Cu metal requires an oxidizing agent.

provenance.evidence_detail: Cu hydroxide amphoterism trap, severity high.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects both (b) and (c) because Cu(OH)2 dissolves in excess NaOH.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Cu(OH)2 marginal amphoterism is the main trap; rejecting Cu metal is essential.

items.title: Rejects Ag
items.description: The response states or implies that option (d) Ag does not dissolve in hot concentrated NaOH because Ag2O is basic, not amphoteric.

provenance.evidence_detail: Ag dissolving misconception trap, severity medium.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects (d) Ag because Ag dissolves in aqua regia or cyanide solutions.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Eliminates confusion between NaOH and reagents like aqua regia or NaCN.

items.title: Fe hydroxides basic
items.description: The response states that Fe(OH)2 or Fe(OH)3 is basic and insoluble in excess NaOH, explaining why Fe is rejected.

provenance.evidence_detail: Fe acid-base confusion trap notes Fe(OH)2/Fe(OH)3 are basic and insoluble.
provenance.discriminates: A response that rejects Fe but for a wrong reason (e.g., passivation alone without noting basic hydroxides).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds chemical depth to the rejection of Fe; supports the amphoteric filter.

items.title: Ag2O is basic
items.description: The response states that Ag2O is basic rather than amphoteric, explaining why Ag does not dissolve in hot concentrated NaOH.

provenance.evidence_detail: Ag dissolving misconception trap notes Ag2O is basic, not amphoteric.
provenance.discriminates: A response that rejects Ag but gives no chemical basis or a wrong basis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Reinforces rejection of Ag with specific compound property.

items.title: Cu metal needs oxidizer
items.description: The response distinguishes Cu metal from Cu(OH)2 by stating Cu metal does not dissolve in hot concentrated NaOH without an oxidizing agent.

provenance.evidence_detail: Cu hydroxide amphoterism trap; correct result notes Cu metal does not dissolve without an oxidizing agent.
provenance.discriminates: A response that rejects Cu but does not distinguish Cu metal from its amphoteric hydroxide.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Addresses the key disputed point: Cu(OH)2 amphoterism vs Cu metal inertness.

items.title: Checks all four
items.description: The response individually evaluates Fe, Zn, Cu, and Ag for dissolution in hot concentrated NaOH rather than stopping after confirming Zn.

provenance.evidence_detail: Single-answer assumption trap, severity low.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects (b) without verifying the other three metals.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Demonstrates complete elimination of all distractors.

items.title: Delta heat indicator
items.description: The response indicates the application of heat (Δ) as a condition for the Zn + 2NaOH reaction.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference equation includes \xrightarrow{\Delta} to denote heating.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the equation without any indication that heat is applied.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Matches the reference equation notation; minor but precise.

items.title: Avoids hydroxo notation
items.description: Avoids writing the product exclusively as Na2[Zn(OH)4] with H2O as a co-reactant when the canonical form for dissolution in hot concentrated NaOH is Na2ZnO2.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts added 2H2O as a co-reactant; the reference omits explicit water on the reactant side.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes Zn + 2NaOH + 2H2O → Na2[Zn(OH)4] + H2 instead of the canonical Na2ZnO2 form.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The IIT-JEE 1980 expected form is Na2ZnO2; hydroxo notation is not wrong but mismatches the question.

items.title: Modulus-one determinant
items.description: The response states that for a unitary matrix, |det U|^2 = 1, or equivalently det U = e^{iα} where α is a real number.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) asks for the general constraint on det(U) for a unitary matrix; the reference derives |det U|² = 1 and det U = e^{iα}.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives a wrong modulus (e.g., det U = 1) or omits the general property entirely.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core result; without it the entire answer fails.

items.title: Derivation starting point
items.description: The response begins the derivation from det(UU dagger) = det(1) = 1, using the unitary property UU dagger = 1.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly shows the chain det(UU†) = det 1 = 1 and det U† = (det U)* leading to |det U|² = 1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts |det U| = 1 without connecting it to the unitary condition UU† = I.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key derivation step anchoring the result in unitarity.

items.title: Conjugate determinant property
items.description: The response uses the property det U dagger = (det U)* in deriving |det U|^2 = 1.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly shows the chain det(UU†) = det 1 = 1 and det U† = (det U)* leading to |det U|² = 1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts |det U| = 1 without connecting it to the unitary condition UU† = I.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required conjugate property linking U and U dagger determinants.

items.title: Matrix-exponential identity
items.description: The response states that det(exp(iF)) = exp(i Tr F) for the operator U = exp(iF) with Hermitian F.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) asks to calculate det(U) explicitly for U = exp(iF); the reference gives det U = exp(i Tr F).
provenance.discriminates: A response that uses a wrong identity such as det(exp(A)) = exp(det A) or det(exp(A)) = Tr(exp A).
provenance.calibration_rationale: Essential identity for the explicit calculation requested.

items.title: Eigenvalue spectrum form
items.description: The response expresses det U = exp(i Σ_k λ_k), where λ_k are the eigenvalues of the Hermitian matrix F with a known spectrum.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts express the determinant in terms of the eigenvalues of F as exp(i Σ λ_k); the question specifies F has a known spectrum.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes the product of eigenvalues of F directly (e.g., λ_1·λ_2···λ_N) instead of the exponential of the sum.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects the identity to F's known spectrum as the question asks.

items.title: Hermitian real spectrum
items.description: The response states that since F is Hermitian, its eigenvalues are real, so i Tr F is purely imaginary and det U is a phase.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus finding: all rollouts note F is Hermitian with real eigenvalues by the spectral theorem; the question states F is Hermitian with a known spectrum.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats eigenvalues of F as potentially complex, losing the phase property of det U.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Justifies why det U is a phase; supports the main result.

items.title: Scalar c formula
items.description: The response gives the scalar c = e^{-iα/N}, where α is real and N is the matrix rank, for the transform U' = cU.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Sign error in exponent phase', severity high: using +iα/N gives det(U') = e^{2iα} ≠ 1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that picks the wrong sign in the exponent of c.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The specific scalar formula is the core of the transform proof.

items.title: Scalar multiplication rule
items.description: The response uses det(cU) = c^N det(U) with N the matrix dimension when computing det U'.

provenance.evidence_detail: The mined pitfall 'Missing dimension factor in det(cU)' flags the common mistake of writing det(cU) = c·det(U).
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes det(cU) = c det(U) instead of c^N det(U), leading to a wrong c.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required determinant rule for scalar multiplication; common pitfall location.

items.title: Explicit unimodular verification
items.description: The response explicitly verifies that det(U') = c^N det(U) = e^{-iα} · e^{iα} = 1, yielding a unimodular matrix.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (c) demands a proof that det(U') = 1; the reference states 'we indeed have det U' = 1'.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts the result without showing the cancellation c^N · det(U) = 1.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The explicit verification is what the question asks to prove.

items.title: Unitarity preserved
items.description: The response notes that |c| = 1 since c = e^{-iα/N} is a pure phase, so the transformed matrix U' = cU remains unitary.

provenance.evidence_detail: The mined pitfall 'Not preserving unitarity of U'' notes that |c| = 1 should be verified to keep U' unitary.
provenance.discriminates: A response that chooses a non-unit-modulus c without acknowledging the unitarity constraint.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Valuable observation that the transform preserves unitarity; not strictly required.

items.title: Existence from real phase
items.description: The response connects the existence of c to the fact that det U = e^{iα} with α real, ensuring the Nth root e^{-iα/N} always exists.

provenance.evidence_detail: The mined pitfall 'Incomplete existence proof' flags responses that give the formula without justifying that the root always exists.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states c = (det U)^{-1/N} without linking it to the phase form det U = e^{iα}.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key logical link between the phase result and the existence proof.

items.title: Avoids wrong det(exp) identity
items.description: Avoids writing det(exp(iF)) = exp(det(iF)) or det(exp(iF)) = Tr(exp(iF)) instead of the correct identity exp(i Tr F).

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong identity for det(exp(A))', severity high: confuses the standard identity with other trace-determinant relations.
provenance.discriminates: A response that applies a muddled formula for the determinant of a matrix exponential.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Named wrong identity; high-impact error if committed.

items.title: Avoids product-of-F-eigenvalues
items.description: Avoids writing det U = ∏_k λ_k (the product of eigenvalues of F) instead of exp(i Σ_k λ_k).

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confusing eigenvalues of F and U', severity medium: the spectral connection is through the exponential.
provenance.discriminates: A response that multiplies eigenvalues of F directly rather than exponentiating and summing.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific wrong move observed; moderate impact on correctness.

items.title: Avoids det U = 1 overclaim
items.description: Avoids stating det U = 1 for a general unitary matrix instead of |det U| = 1 or det U = e^{iα}.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly shows det U = e^{iα}, not 1; a response that claims det U = 1 for all unitary matrices contradicts the reference.
provenance.discriminates: A response that overstates the result by dropping the phase freedom of the determinant.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common overclaim; directly contradicts the correct modulus-one result.

items.title: Multiplicative det step
items.description: The response uses the multiplicative property det(UU dagger) = det U · det U dagger to separate the determinant product.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly shows the chain det(UU†) = det 1 = 1 and det U† = (det U)* leading to |det U|² = 1.
provenance.discriminates: A response that asserts |det U| = 1 without connecting it to the unitary condition UU† = I.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Intermediate algebraic step in the standard derivation.

items.title: Independent-particle limit
items.description: Conventional band theory treats electrons as independent particles in a mean-field potential and does not account for correlated excited states such as excitons.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) target: band theory limitation due to independent-particle approximation and absence of two-particle correlation.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that vaguely says band theory is 'limited' without identifying the independent-particle / missing-correlation cause.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core structural limitation of band theory; directly explains why excitons cannot be predicted.

items.title: Excitons as bound pairs
items.description: Excitons are bound electron-hole pairs that are genuine two-particle correlated states absent from the single-particle band spectrum.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agree excitons are two-particle bound states below the gap, missing from independent-particle eigenstates.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that calls excitons merely 'excited conduction-band states' without the bound-pair / two-particle character.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Defines what excitons are; foundational for explaining their absence from band theory.

items.title: Correlations bind excitons
items.description: Electron correlations produce the attractive electron-hole interaction that binds excitons, and because conventional band theory ignores these correlations, excitons cannot appear in the single-particle spectrum.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) target: role of electron correlations in creating attractive electron-hole interaction.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that attributes exciton absence to band theory being 'too simple' without naming electron correlations.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Links correlations to binding mechanism and causally explains why band theory fails.

items.title: Effective mass kinematic
items.description: The effective mass concept parametrizes band dispersion and does not generate the Coulomb attraction that binds excitons, so the effective mass approximation alone cannot produce excitonic bound states within conventional band theory.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Effective mass suffices' (severity high): conflating parametrization with binding mechanism.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says band theory plus effective masses yields excitons.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly addresses the effective mass concept as requested; distinguishes kinematics from binding.

items.title: Hydrogenic reduced mass
items.description: The effective mass enters the description of excitons through the reduced mass μ = m_e* m_h*/(m_e* + m_h*) in the hydrogenic model, where the Coulomb attraction uses the material dielectric constant ε rather than the vacuum value.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Unscreened hydrogenic formula' (severity medium): using ε = 1 gives binding energies orders of magnitude too large.
provenance.discriminates: A response that writes the hydrogenic exciton formula with ε = 1 as if the solid were vacuum.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specifies the reduced mass formula and dielectric screening; adds concrete depth.

items.title: On-site U in formation
items.description: The on-site Coulomb interaction U contributes to the formation of excitons in realistic materials by influencing the binding strength and localization of electron-hole pairs.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly states on-site Coulomb interaction U plays 'a crucial role' in exciton formation.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that discusses mechanisms but never identifies on-site U as crucial to exciton formation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly answers the sub-question on how on-site U influences exciton formation.

items.title: U attractive in e-h channel
items.description: The on-site Coulomb interaction U, when viewed in the electron-hole channel, transmutes into an attractive interaction that binds localized (Frenkel-type) excitons, rather than remaining repulsive as it is for two electrons.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Sign of U in e-h channel' (severity high): U transmutes to attraction under particle-hole transformation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims on-site U destabilizes or opposes exciton binding.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key mechanism: U becomes attractive in electron-hole channel; prevents sign misconception.

items.title: Screening renormalizes U
items.description: In realistic materials the on-site Coulomb interaction is screened to U_eff ≈ U/ε, where ε is the material dielectric constant, rather than the bare unscreened U directly setting the exciton binding energy.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Ignoring screening' (severity medium): unscreened U gives unrealistically large binding energies.
provenance.discriminates: A response that predicts eV-scale binding from bare U without dielectric screening.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Screening formula U_eff ≈ U/ε is concrete and essential for realistic materials.

items.title: Screening sets exciton type
items.description: Weak screening and large effective U yield tightly bound Frenkel excitons, while strong screening and small U yield Wannier-Mott excitons.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agree: weak screening + large U → Frenkel; strong screening + modest U → Wannier-Mott.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that discusses U but never connects screening strength to exciton type or localization.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects screening strength to exciton type; covers Frenkel vs Wannier-Mott distinction.

items.title: Beyond-band-theory methods
items.description: Methods beyond conventional band theory such as the Bethe-Salpeter equation or configuration interaction include the missing electron-hole interaction kernel that conventional band theory lacks.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts mention BSE and configuration interaction as methods including the electron-hole kernel.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that says correlations are needed but never identifies any formalism that supplies them.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Names concrete methods that capture excitons; confirms what band theory cannot do.

items.title: U in BSE kernel
items.description: The on-site Coulomb interaction U enters the attractive direct term of the electron-hole interaction kernel, such as in the BSE kernel, directly setting the exciton binding strength.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollout 3 explicitly notes U enters the BSE kernel direct term; rollouts 1 and 2 omit this detail.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that discusses U only as a gap renormalization without its role in the binding kernel.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specifies how U enters the BSE kernel; adds depth on binding mechanism.

items.title: Correlations vs mean-field
items.description: Electron correlations requiring explicit two-particle treatment are distinct from single-particle mean-field corrections such as Hartree-Fock exchange or DFT self-energies.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Correlations vs. exchange-only': exchange is mean-field, excitons need two-particle ladder diagrams.
provenance.discriminates: An answer that presents exchange or LDA corrections as sufficient for excitonic effects.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Distinguishes correlations from mean-field corrections; clarifies why exchange is insufficient.

items.title: Pitfall: band eigenstates
items.description: Avoids arguing that conduction-band eigenstates are excited states that include excitons, so conventional band theory should capture them.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Band theory has excited states' (severity high): conflating single-particle excitations with two-particle correlated states.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims band theory already describes excitons via conduction-band states.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Prevents a specific misconception conflating band eigenstates with excitonic states.

items.title: Pitfall: exchange suffices
items.description: Avoids claiming that Hartree-Fock exchange or DFT-LDA corrections to the band structure fully capture excitonic effects.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Correlations vs. exchange-only' (severity medium): exchange is mean-field; excitons need explicit two-particle correlation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says Hartree-Fock or LDA corrections already produce excitons.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Prevents overclaiming that mean-field corrections capture genuine two-particle excitons.

items.title: Pitfall: U as gap only
items.description: Avoids discussing the on-site Coulomb interaction U solely as a quantity that opens a Mott or charge-transfer gap while omitting its role in binding the electron-hole pair.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'U as band-gap renormalization only' (severity low): U both renormalizes gap and binds excitons.
provenance.discriminates: A response that explains U modifies band structure but never its binding role.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Prevents reducing U to gap-opening only; ensures binding role is addressed.
