items.title: Morphine as treatment
items.description: States morphine as the necessary pharmacological treatment for the newborn.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question asks for the necessary pharmacological treatment; the reference answer specifies morphine as first-line therapy for NAS.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names a non-opioid drug or gives no specific agent fails this criterion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; naming morphine inherently covers opioid drug class. Without it the answer fails.

items.title: NAS diagnosis identified
items.description: Identifies the newborn's condition as neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS).

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts and the reference answer identify NAS as the underlying diagnosis from the symptom cluster.
provenance.discriminates: A response that attributes symptoms to sepsis, metabolic disorder, or another neonatal condition fails this criterion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct diagnosis is prerequisite to correct treatment; essential anchor for the entire answer.

items.title: Opioid withdrawal etiology
items.description: Attributes the newborn's symptoms to opioid withdrawal from in utero exposure to opioids.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer links NAS to opioid exposure in utero; all rollouts explicitly make this connection.
provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses NAS but does not connect it to opioid withdrawal, or attributes it to non-opioid substances, fails this criterion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Links cause to diagnosis; key reasoning connecting maternal exposure to newborn presentation.

items.title: Maternal opioid use inferred
items.description: Infers that the mother used opioids during pregnancy despite no explicit substance use history in the stem.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts explicitly note the assumption of maternal opioid use; the reference states withdrawal is due to substances the mother may have used during pregnancy.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states the maternal history is unknown and therefore cannot determine the diagnosis fails to make the necessary clinical inference.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required reasoning step; stem gives no direct history so inference is clinically significant.

items.title: Symptoms mapped to NAS
items.description: Recognizes that the presenting symptoms including irritability, high-pitched crying, diaphoresis, runny nose, and limb flailing align with neonatal abstinence syndrome and that onset several hours after birth supports this diagnosis.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly maps each symptom to NAS; all rollouts correctly associated the symptom cluster with withdrawal.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct treatment without acknowledging how the specific symptoms support the diagnosis lacks the reasoning chain.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Symptom-to-diagnosis mapping adds depth but is secondary to naming the treatment itself.

items.title: Tapering mechanism explained
items.description: Explains that morphine alleviates withdrawal symptoms by gradually tapering dependency.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly states morphine helps by gradually tapering the dependency, a detail no rollout included.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names morphine but does not address the tapering mechanism of action scores lower on clinical depth.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Mechanism detail from reference answer; real added depth but not essential for correctness.

items.title: Methadone as alternative
items.description: Mentions methadone as an alternative opioid for managing withdrawal in newborns.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts identified methadone as an acceptable alternative opioid agonist, though the reference answer focuses on morphine.
provenance.discriminates: A response that only discusses morphine and labels other opioids as incorrect misses the nuance that methadone is also acceptable.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Valid alternative agent; adds pharmacological depth beyond the single correct answer.

items.title: Avoids naloxone recommendation
items.description: Avoids recommending naloxone as pharmacological treatment for the opioid-exposed newborn experiencing neonatal withdrawal symptoms.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall: naloxone is the classic opioid reversal agent but is contraindicated in opioid-dependent neonates as it precipitates acute severe withdrawal.
provenance.discriminates: A response that suggests naloxone to reverse suspected opioid exposure commits a high-severity safety error.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Naloxone would precipitate or worsen withdrawal; dangerous and commonly confused distractor.

items.title: Avoids phenobarbital first-line
items.description: Avoids naming phenobarbital as the first-line pharmacological treatment for opioid neonatal abstinence syndrome.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall: phenobarbital is widely taught for neonatal withdrawal but is reserved for non-opioid or polysubstance withdrawal, not first-line for opioid NAS.
provenance.discriminates: A response that recommends phenobarbital as the primary treatment for opioid withdrawal commits a high-severity error.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Phenobarbital is adjunctive not first-line for opioid NAS; common but lower-stakes misconception.

items.title: Meckel's diverticulum
items.description: The response states that the underlying cause of the clinical findings is a Meckel's diverticulum.

provenance.evidence_detail: The single sub-question asks for the underlying cause; the reference names Meckel's diverticulum.
provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses an enteric duplication cyst or omits the anatomic diagnosis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core diagnosis; without it the answer is wrong. Directly answers the sub-question.
provenance.merged_mirror_text: Avoids stating that intussusception is the underlying cause of the clinical findings rather than a complication of the Meckel's diverticulum.

items.title: Vitelline duct embryology
items.description: The response identifies incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct (omphalomesenteric duct) as the congenital embryologic mechanism producing the diverticulum.

provenance.evidence_detail: Divergence in anatomic detail; reference uses vitelline duct; both synonyms are acceptable.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names neither vitelline nor omphalomesenteric duct.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Embryologic origin is a key tested point; naming only Meckel's without the vitelline duct is incomplete.

items.title: Ectopic gastric tissue in ileum
items.description: The response states that the cystic mass in the ileum contains ectopic gastric tissue, as revealed by the histology report.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim that gastric mucosa is present in the ileum, matching the reference.
provenance.discriminates: A response that does not connect the histology finding of gastric tissue to the lesion.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects histology finding to diagnosis; distinguishes Meckel's from other cystic masses.

items.title: Acid causing ulceration
items.description: The response explains that the ectopic gastric tissue produces acid leading to ulceration of the adjacent ileal mucosa.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Missing bleeding mechanism'; the reference states gastric tissue leads to acid production and subsequent ulceration.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions gastric tissue but does not link it to acid-induced ulceration.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key intermediate mechanism linking gastric tissue to bleeding; a common omission.

items.title: Bleeding mechanism
items.description: The response states that the dark red stools are due to bleeding from the ulcerated ileal mucosa.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly links ulceration to dark red stools due to bleeding; linkage detail beyond bare diagnosis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that lists dark stools without explaining the bleeding mechanism.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains the presenting symptom of dark red stools through the ulceration pathway.

items.title: Intussusception as complication
items.description: The response identifies intussusception, described as the bowel telescoping into itself, as the mechanism causing the intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference links intermittent pain and vomiting to possible intussusception consistent with imaging.
provenance.discriminates: A response that attributes obstruction to the diverticulum directly without naming intussusception.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains obstructive symptoms; distinguishes complication from underlying cause.

items.title: Diverticulum as lead point
items.description: The response states that the Meckel's diverticulum acts as a lead point for the intussusception.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim that the diverticulum acts as a lead point causing the bowel to telescope.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions intussusception but does not identify the diverticulum as the lead point.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects the diverticulum to the intussusception mechanism, completing the causal chain.

items.title: Imaging findings consistent
items.description: The response interprets the air fluid levels on CT as consistent with bowel obstruction from the intussusception.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus interpretation of the CT finding of air fluid levels as obstruction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions air fluid levels without linking them to obstruction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Integrates imaging data with the diagnosis; adds depth but not essential to the answer.

items.title: Avoids urachus as origin
items.description: Avoids citing persistence of the urachus as the embryologic origin of the ileal cystic mass.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong embryologic duct'; high severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims the mass is due to a patent urachus remnant.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Names a specific wrong embryologic structure; a plausible but incorrect distractor.

items.title: Avoids duplication cyst
items.description: Avoids diagnosing the cystic mass in the ileum as an intestinal duplication cyst rather than a Meckel's diverticulum.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Misnaming the lesion'; medium severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims the underlying cause is an enteric duplication cyst.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common differential trap; both can contain ectopic tissue but embryologic origins differ.

items.title: Morton's neuroma diagnosis
items.description: The response states the most likely diagnosis is Morton's neuroma.

provenance.evidence_detail: The single required deliverable is the most likely diagnosis, which is Morton's neuroma per the reference answer.
provenance.discriminates: Any response giving an alternative diagnosis such as metatarsalgia, tarsal tunnel syndrome, or stress fracture.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; diagnosis is the single required quantity for this question.

items.title: 3rd/4th interspace localization
items.description: The response localizes the Morton's neuroma to the area between the third and fourth metatarsals.

provenance.evidence_detail: The rollouts disagreed on whether to specify the interspace; the reference answer explicitly states 'between the third and fourth metatarsals'.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states Morton's neuroma but gives the wrong interspace (e.g., 2nd intermetatarsal space) or omits the location entirely.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific interspace is a key distinguishing feature of this case presentation.

items.title: Burning plantar pain cited
items.description: The response cites the burning sensation in the plantar area as a supporting clinical finding for Morton's neuroma.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly identifies 'a burning sensation in the plantar area' as characteristic of the condition.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names the diagnosis but does not connect it to the plantar burning symptom described in the case.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Burning plantar pain is a hallmark symptom anchoring the diagnosis.

items.title: Radiation to 3rd/4th digits
items.description: The response mentions pain that radiates to the third and fourth digits or toes as a supporting feature of Morton's neuroma.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts and the reference agree that radiation to the 3rd and 4th digits is a key supporting clinical feature.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits the radiation pattern and gives only a bare diagnosis without clinical correlation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Radiation pattern narrows the diagnosis to the involved nerve distribution.

items.title: Mulder's click identified
items.description: The response identifies the notable clicking sound on pressure between the metatarsal heads as Mulder's click or Mulder's sign.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly names 'Mulder's click' as a finding that further supports the diagnosis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions the click but does not name it Mulder's sign, or fails to mention the click finding at all.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Mulder's sign is a pathognomonic exam finding for Morton's neuroma.

items.title: Tenderness between metatarsal heads
items.description: The response cites the pain with pressure between the metatarsal heads as a supporting physical exam finding.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer references pressure applied between the metatarsal heads in the context of Mulder's click.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names the diagnosis but does not connect it to the palpation tenderness finding.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Supports diagnosis but overlaps with Mulder's click criterion.

items.title: Nerve thickening pathophysiology
items.description: The response describes Morton's neuroma as involving thickening of the tissue around the interdigital nerve between the metatarsals.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus_correct list notes Morton's neuroma is also called interdigital neuroma.
provenance.discriminates: A response that does not specify the nerve structure affected, giving only a label without anatomical basis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds mechanistic depth; merges nerve involvement and thickening descriptions.

items.title: Tinel's sign correctly labeled
items.description: The response identifies the pain referral to the third and fourth digits on tapping as Tinel's sign and avoids labeling the click as Tinel's or the tap pain as Mulder's sign.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus_correct list includes 'Pain on tapping corresponds to Tinel's sign', though the reference answer omits the eponym by name.
provenance.discriminates: A response that swaps the eponyms, labeling the tapping pain as Mulder's sign.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct eponym assignment adds precision; absorbs eponym-swap avoidance.

items.title: Vascular and skin exclusion
items.description: The response notes that palpable posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses and intact skin help exclude vascular and dermatologic etiologies.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus_correct list includes that intact skin and pulses exclude vascular/dermatologic etiology.
provenance.discriminates: A response that ignores the vascular exam findings and does not use them to narrow the differential.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real but peripheral reasoning; merges two exclusionary-finding items.

items.title: Right foot and 3-month duration
items.description: The response acknowledges that the right foot pain has been present for 3 months, consistent with a chronic condition such as Morton's neuroma.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question stem specifies right foot pain for 3 months; the reference answer describes the 45-year-old woman's presentation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that fails to acknowledge the affected side documented in the question stem.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Minor case-specific detail; merges laterality and duration items.

items.title: Avoids tarsal tunnel syndrome
items.description: Avoids diagnosing tarsal tunnel syndrome instead of Morton's neuroma between the third and fourth metatarsals.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Tarsal tunnel mislocalization' — high severity confusion between medial ankle entrapment and plantar interdigital entrapment.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mislocalizes the entrapment to the medial ankle/tarsal tunnel.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common differential trap; tarsal tunnel involves medial ankle not plantar interspace.

items.title: Avoids metatarsalgia diagnosis
items.description: Avoids diagnosing generalized or primary metatarsalgia instead of Morton's neuroma as the most likely diagnosis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Metatarsalgia confusion' — high severity temptation to anchor on tenderness between metatarsal heads.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives 'metatarsalgia' as the final diagnosis while ignoring the burning, radiating neuropathic pain and Mulder's click.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Metatarsalgia lacks the neuropathic burning, radiation, and Mulder's click seen here.

items.title: Avoids wrong interspace
items.description: Avoids stating the Morton's neuroma is in the 2nd intermetatarsal space between the 2nd and 3rd metatarsals.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong interspace stated' — low severity default-to-2nd-space error.
provenance.discriminates: A response that incorrectly specifies the 2nd intermetatarsal space rather than the 3rd.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Case specifically anchors the lesion to the 3rd intermetatarsal space.

items.title: Correct answer A
items.description: The response selects A. Ketoconazole as the drug unlikely to reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Answering opposite question': reading the stem as asking which drug does reduce OC effectiveness.
provenance.discriminates: A response that picks an anticonvulsant because it misread the question direction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Selecting the correct option is indispensable; absorbed the inverse pitfall.

items.title: Ketoconazole inhibits CYP450
items.description: The response states that Ketoconazole inhibits CYP450 (CYP3A4) liver enzymes rather than inducing them.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Inducer vs inhibitor confusion': classifying ketoconazole as a CYP450 inducer rather than a CYP3A4 inhibitor.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says ketoconazole induces liver enzymes or would lower OC levels.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core mechanism distinguishing ketoconazole from the anticonvulsants.

items.title: Inhibition stabilizes OC levels
items.description: The response states that Ketoconazole inhibition would potentially stabilize or increase oral contraceptives levels rather than decrease them.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly states ketoconazole could stabilize or increase OC levels rather than decrease them.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims CYP450 inhibition reduces OC effectiveness by lowering hormone levels.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains why inhibition does not reduce OC effectiveness.

items.title: Anticonvulsants as inducers
items.description: The response identifies Phenytoin, Phenobarbital, and Carbamazepine as CYP450 enzyme inducers that reduce oral contraceptives effectiveness.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer lists phenytoin among the enzyme inducers that reduce OC effectiveness; all rollouts agree.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims phenytoin does not reduce OC effectiveness or misclassifies it as an inhibitor.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Covers all three wrong-options' shared mechanism; merged four duplicates.

items.title: Induction lowers OC levels
items.description: The response explains that CYP450 enzyme induction speeds up the metabolism of oral contraceptives, thereby reducing their effectiveness.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer states that phenytoin, phenobarbital, and carbamazepine are enzyme inducers that speed up metabolism of contraceptives, thereby reducing effectiveness.
provenance.discriminates: A response that identifies the correct drug but gives no mechanism or a wrong mechanism for reduced OC effectiveness.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Names CYP450 as the mechanism linking induction to reduced OC efficacy.

items.title: Contrast inhibitor vs inducers
items.description: The response draws a contrast between Ketoconazole as an enzyme inhibitor and Phenytoin, Phenobarbital, and Carbamazepine as enzyme inducers.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly contrasts ketoconazole (inhibitor) with the other three options (inducers).
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct letter but does not distinguish inhibitor from inducer mechanisms.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Synthesis that ties the correct and incorrect options together.

items.title: Avoids anticonvulsant misclassification
items.description: Avoids treating Phenytoin, Phenobarbital, or Carbamazepine as CYP450 inhibitors rather than enzyme inducers.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Anticonvulsant class error': treating one of the three anticonvulsants as a non-inducer.
provenance.discriminates: A response that claims one of the anticonvulsants does not reduce OC effectiveness.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific trap observed in flawed responses; guards against role reversal.

items.title: Avoids gut flora myth
items.description: Avoids arguing that Ketoconazole reduces oral contraceptives effectiveness via gut flora or enterohepatic recirculation disruption.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Broad-spectrum antibiotic myth': confusing ketoconazole's CYP3A4 inhibition with the rifampin/antibiotic enterohepatic mechanism.
provenance.discriminates: A response that applies an antibiotic-OC interaction mechanism to ketoconazole.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Distinct mechanistic misconception; lower weight as secondary trap.

items.title: OCs are active drugs
items.description: The response indicates that oral contraceptives are active drugs whose levels are not reduced by CYP450 inhibition because they do not require metabolic activation.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Reversed interaction direction' notes OCs are active drugs, not prodrugs, so CYP inhibition does not reduce their efficacy.
provenance.discriminates: A response that implies OC hormones are prodrugs requiring CYP-mediated activation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds mechanistic depth explaining why inhibition is not a problem.

items.title: Coronary flow peak
items.description: States that coronary flow is at its peak at the end of ventricular diastole.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) asks for the direction/magnitude of coronary flow at end-diastole; reference states it is 'optimal' and 'at its peak.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that says coronary flow decreases or is low at end-diastole.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer for first sub-question; highest importance, expected high discrimination.

items.title: Aortic flow minimal
items.description: States that aortic flow is minimal at the end of ventricular diastole.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) asks for the direction/magnitude of aortic flow at end-diastole; reference states it is 'minimal' because the aortic valve is closed.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says aortic flow is high or increasing at end-diastole.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer for second sub-question; highest importance, expected high discrimination.

items.title: Ventricles relaxed
items.description: States that the ventricles are fully relaxed at the end of ventricular diastole.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts and the reference agree that ventricles are fully relaxed at end-diastole, which is the mechanistic basis for high coronary flow.
provenance.discriminates: A response that describes the ventricles as contracting or partially contracted at end-diastole.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key mechanism explaining why coronary flow peaks; addresses common error.

items.title: Coronary not compressed
items.description: States that coronary arteries are not compressed by the relaxed ventricles, allowing blood to supply the heart muscle.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus across rollouts: low intramyocardial pressure and minimized extravascular compression explain high coronary flow; reference states ventricles are 'not compressed by the contracting heart.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct coronary flow value but provides no mechanism or a wrong mechanism.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains the mechanism for peak coronary flow; addresses collective error.

items.title: Aortic valve closed
items.description: States that the aortic valve remains closed at the end of ventricular diastole, preventing blood from flowing back into the heart.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts and the reference explicitly state the aortic valve is closed during ventricular diastole.
provenance.discriminates: A response that implies or states the aortic valve opens before the onset of systole.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key mechanism for minimal aortic flow; merges valve-closed and backflow-prevention facts.

items.title: Pressure gradient mechanism
items.description: States that coronary flow is at peak because pressure in the aorta during diastole exceeds intramyocardial pressure when the ventricles are relaxed.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts mention that aortic diastolic pressure exceeds intramyocardial pressure during ventricular relaxation as the mechanism for high coronary flow.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states coronary flow is high but explains it with a wrong pressure relationship, e.g., that ventricular pressure drives coronary flow.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Deeper mechanistic reasoning; adds correctness depth beyond the core answer.

items.title: Ventricles filled ready
items.description: States that the ventricles are filled with blood and ready to contract at the end of ventricular diastole.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states 'the ventricles are filled with blood and ready to contract'; rollouts did not explicitly mention the filled-and-ready state.
provenance.discriminates: A response that describes coronary and aortic flow but fails to anchor the end-diastolic state to maximal ventricular filling.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Supports the transition to systole; contextual correctness anchor.

items.title: Aortic flow standby
items.description: States that aortic flow is on standby, prepared to begin with the onset of systole.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states 'aortic flow is on standby, prepared to begin with the onset of systole'; rollouts did not use this transitional framing.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says aortic flow is zero without noting it will resume at the onset of systole.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds transitional framing; lower discrimination expected but real depth.

items.title: Diastole-systole transition
items.description: States that as ventricular diastole concludes and transitions into systole, the aortic valve will soon open to initiate blood flow into the aorta.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference provides a forward-looking statement about the transition to systole and impending aortic valve opening; rollouts focused only on the instantaneous end-diastolic state.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers both sub-questions but omits any mention of the impending transition to systole.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Predictive transition; real added depth but not essential to the answer.

items.title: Coronary diastolic dominance
items.description: States that coronary blood flow occurs during diastole rather than systole.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Coronary flow timing reversed' identifies the misconception that coronary flow peaks during systole; stating the general diastolic-dominance principle prevents this error.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct end-diastolic value but does not articulate the general principle that coronary perfusion is diastolic.
provenance.calibration_rationale: General principle underpinning the peak; reinforces correctness.

items.title: Avoids coronary systolic peak
items.description: Avoids stating that coronary flow is low at the end of ventricular diastole because the heart is not contracting.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Coronary flow timing reversed' (high severity): the intuition that flow to an organ should be highest when it is working hardest leads to the incorrect claim that coronary flow is low at end-diastole.
provenance.discriminates: A response that correctly identifies the end-diastolic phase but reverses the coronary flow direction, claiming it is suppressed because the heart is relaxed.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Direct inversion of the correct answer; likely high observed discrimination.

items.title: Avoids early aortic flow
items.description: Avoids claiming that aortic flow begins or increases at the end of ventricular diastole, including by attributing it to atrial contraction.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfalls 'Aortic valve opened early' (high) and 'Atrial systole ejects to aorta' (high): end-diastole is adjacent to systole, and atrial contraction is easily conflated with ventricular ejection, leading to the false claim that aortic flow starts during late diastole.
provenance.discriminates: A response that blurs the diastole-systole boundary and claims atrial systole or ventricular preparation causes aortic flow before the aortic valve opens.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common misconception tying aortic flow to wrong phase; specific trap.

items.title: Avoids runoff conflation
items.description: Avoids treating aortic flow across the aortic valve as the same as continued peripheral runoff within the aorta during diastole.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Aortic flow vs aortic runoff' (medium severity): the windkessel effect causes genuine forward movement of blood within the aorta during diastole, but flow across the aortic valve is zero; responses that report aortic flow as non-zero because of peripheral runoff are making a distinct conceptual error.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says aortic flow is moderate or non-zero because blood continues flowing through the aorta to the periphery, rather than distinguishing valve flow from intravascular runoff.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific conceptual trap conflating valve flow with intra-aortic runoff.

items.title: Acute gout diagnosis
items.description: Identifies the patient's condition as acute gout (acute gouty arthritis).

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) requires identifying the likely diagnosis from the clinical presentation of painful swollen great toe with gout risk factors.
provenance.discriminates: A response that misidentifies the condition as cellulitis, septic arthritis, or pseudogout and therefore proceeds down the wrong pharmacologic path.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core diagnosis grounding the entire answer; without it the mechanism is baseless.

items.title: Colchicine identification
items.description: Identifies the new medication as colchicine.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) requires implicit identification of the drug from the described effects (decreases leukocyte migration and mitosis; nausea/vomiting).
provenance.discriminates: A response that names allopurinol, an NSAID, or a glucocorticoid instead of colchicine.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Naming the correct drug is prerequisite to stating its mechanism of action.

items.title: Binds tubulin
items.description: States that the mechanism of action involves binding to tubulin, specifically β-tubulin.

provenance.evidence_detail: One rollout specified β-tubulin while others used generic 'tubulin'; the reference is silent on subunit specificity but does not contradict β-tubulin.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states only generic 'tubulin' without the more precise β-tubulin subunit identification.
provenance.calibration_rationale: The molecular target is the crux of the mechanism question; high importance.

items.title: Inhibits microtubule formation
items.description: States that the mechanism of action is inhibition of microtubule formation.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) targets the molecular mechanism; the reference answer states 'inhibition of microtubule formation.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that states colchicine stabilizes microtubules (taxane-like) rather than inhibiting their formation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Functional consequence of tubulin binding; directly answers the question asked.

items.title: Decreased leukocyte migration
items.description: States that colchicine reduces inflammation by decreasing leukocyte migration.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) requires describing the cellular consequence of the mechanism; the question stem and reference both mention decreased leukocyte migration.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states the molecular target but does not connect it to the anti-inflammatory effect on leukocytes.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Links mechanism to clinical effect described in the question stem; key intermediate.

items.title: Microtubule-dependent leukocyte function
items.description: States that the mechanism interferes with microtubule-dependent functions in leukocytes.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) requires connecting the molecular target (microtubule) to the cellular effect (leukocyte dysfunction); this intermediate claim bridges criteria 3/4 and 5/6.
provenance.discriminates: A response that lists tubulin binding and leukocyte migration separately without connecting them through microtubule-dependent function.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects tubulin binding to leukocyte effects; adds mechanistic depth beyond migration.

items.title: Decreased mitosis
items.description: States that the mechanism decreases mitosis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (b) requires describing the cellular consequence; the question stem and reference both mention decreased mitosis as part of colchicine's effect.
provenance.discriminates: A response that discusses leukocyte migration but omits the antimitotic effect that explains both efficacy and GI toxicity.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explicitly stated in the question stem and reference answer; required intermediate result.

items.title: GI toxicity rationale
items.description: Explains nausea and vomiting as due to effects on rapidly dividing cells in the gastrointestinal tract.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference answer explicitly attributes GI side effects to effects on rapidly dividing cells in the GI tract; not all rollout attempts included this rationale.
provenance.discriminates: A response that lists nausea and vomiting as side effects without explaining the mechanism by which colchicine injures rapidly dividing GI epithelial cells.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains side effects referenced in the case; real added depth but not the central question.

items.title: Acute gout therapy
items.description: States that colchicine is used to treat the acute attack of gout rather than chronic urate-lowering therapy.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confuses acute with chronic gout therapy' identifies the risk of naming allopurinol or febuxostat; this criterion positively anchors the correct classification.
provenance.discriminates: A response that frames the medication as chronic urate-lowering therapy or does not distinguish acute from chronic use.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Distinguishes acute treatment from chronic prophylaxis; contextually relevant but not the mechanism.

items.title: Avoids xanthine oxidase inhibitor
items.description: Avoids identifying the medication as allopurinol or febuxostat and stating the mechanism as xanthine oxidase inhibition.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confuses acute with chronic gout therapy' (severity: high) — hydrochlorothiazide and alcohol clues steer toward urate-lowering drugs.
provenance.discriminates: A response that identifies allopurinol or febuxostat as the medication and gives xanthine oxidase inhibition as the mechanism.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common wrong-drug pitfall for gout; discriminates correct acute therapy from chronic prophylaxis.

items.title: Avoids NSAID or glucocorticoid
items.description: Avoids identifying the medication as an NSAID or glucocorticoid and stating the mechanism as COX inhibition or phospholipase A2 inhibition.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confuses colchicine with NSAIDs' (severity: high) — NSAIDs are the most common first-line for acute gout.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names indomethacin or another NSAID and gives COX/prostaglandin inhibition as the mechanism.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Alternative acute gout drugs with different mechanisms; merging covers both wrong-drug paths.

items.title: Avoids wrong microtubule mechanism
items.description: Avoids stating that colchicine stabilizes or promotes microtubule polymerization rather than inhibiting it, or naming kinesin or dynein as the binding target instead of tubulin.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'States microtubule stabilization instead of inhibition' (severity: medium) — taxanes stabilize microtubules, creating a sign-reversed conflation.
provenance.discriminates: A response that correctly identifies microtubules but reverses the directionality, describing stabilization or promotion rather than inhibition.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly targets the mechanism question; catches reversal of direction or wrong molecular target.

items.title: Identifies H. influenzae
items.description: The response identifies Haemophilus influenzae as the causative agent responsible for this infection.

provenance.evidence_detail: The single sub-question asks the student to name the causative organism; the reference answer gives Haemophilus influenzae.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers Neisseria meningitidis, Bordetella pertussis, or gives no organism name.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without naming the organism correctness collapses entirely.

items.title: Diagnoses bacterial meningitis
items.description: The response states that the presentation of fever, vomiting, and neck rigidity in a 2-year-old child indicates bacterial meningitis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus across all rollouts and reference that the presentation equals acute bacterial meningitis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that calls this viral meningitis or aseptic meningitis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key clinical reasoning linking presentation to diagnosis; high discriminative importance.

items.title: Interprets CSF profile
items.description: The response interprets the CSF analysis showing over 200 polymorphs/ml, 100 mg/dl protein, and 10 mg/dl glucose as consistent with bacterial meningitis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim linking the CSF values to bacterial etiology.
provenance.discriminates: A response that ignores the CSF values or labels them as normal or viral.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required intermediate result anchoring the bacterial etiology from lab data.

items.title: States Gram-negative coccobacilli
items.description: The response states that the Gram's stain reveals Gram-negative coccobacilli as the microscopic morphology of the causative organism.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim that Gram-negative coccobacilli is a key clue.
provenance.discriminates: A response that describes the organism as Gram-negative diplococci or Gram-positive.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Critical microbiologic clue distinguishing Haemophilus from other meningitis pathogens.

items.title: Chocolate agar only growth
items.description: The response states that the bacterial culture grows on chocolate agar but does not grow on blood agar.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus correct claim about chocolate agar growth.
provenance.discriminates: A response that says the organism does not grow on chocolate agar.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Definitive culture pattern for H. influenzae; merging both agar facts into one checkable item.

items.title: Explains X and V factors
items.description: The response explains that Haemophilus influenzae requires factor X and factor V growth factors, which are present in chocolate agar because lysed RBCs release them.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus across all rollouts and the reference that X and V factors explain chocolate agar growth.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives no growth factor explanation or cites wrong factors.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Mechanistic explanation linking chocolate agar growth to the organism's requirements.

items.title: Names factor X and V
items.description: The response identifies factor X as hemin and factor V as NAD, both supplied by chocolate agar.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong growth factors cited' warns that X and V can be swapped.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels factor X as NAD or swaps the two factor identities.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Added depth on the specific growth factor identities; real but not essential for diagnosis.

items.title: Links age to type b
items.description: The response links the 2-year-old child age and meningitis presentation to Haemophilus influenzae type b as the causative pathogen.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts specified type b; the reference answer implies it by context of pediatric meningitis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names only the species without the type, or names the wrong type.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Age-pathogen association strengthens the diagnosis; clinically important for pediatric meningitis.

items.title: Avoids blood agar growth claim
items.description: The response avoids reversing the culture results by claiming the organism grows on blood agar, whether by stating a reversed pattern or by invoking satellite growth around Staphylococcus aureus.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Reversed agar growth pattern' flagged as high severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that swaps the chocolate agar and blood agar growth findings.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Merges two related pitfall mechanisms; both rationalize incorrect blood agar growth for H. influenzae.

items.title: Avoids Bordetella pertussis
items.description: The response avoids selecting Bordetella pertussis, which is a Gram-negative coccobacillus and pediatric pathogen but does not cause meningitis and does not grow on chocolate agar.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Confused with Bordetella pertussis' flagged as medium severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers Bordetella pertussis based on shared morphology.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Plausible morphologic distractor; correct response distinguishes by clinical syndrome and culture.

items.title: Diagnosis of bacterial meningitis
items.description: The response states that the presentation of fever, vomiting, and neck rigidity in a 2-year-old child indicates bacterial meningitis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus across all rollouts and reference that the presentation equals acute bacterial meningitis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that calls this viral meningitis or aseptic meningitis.

items.title: Diagnosis: communicating hydrocele
items.description: States the likely diagnosis for the 3-year-old child is a communicating hydrocele.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question asks to identify the likely diagnosis; reference answer and all three rollouts agree on communicating hydrocele.
provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses generic hydrocele, torsion, hernia, or any other condition.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without this the response is wrong. Highest importance.

items.title: Transillumination means fluid-filled
items.description: States that the positive transillumination test indicates the swelling is fluid-filled.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference explicitly states positive transillumination indicates fluid-filled swelling; consensus among rollouts as well.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions transillumination but does not explain it indicates fluid content.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key diagnostic finding linking transillumination to fluid; central to correct diagnosis.

items.title: Fluid around testicle
items.description: States that the scrotal swelling is due to fluid around the testicle.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference describes 'fluid around the testicle' as the cause of scrotal swelling.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names the diagnosis but does not describe the underlying pathology of fluid accumulation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Defines the pathological basis of the hydrocele; supports diagnosis but less critical than the test interpretation.

items.title: Fluid drains when supine
items.description: States that fluid tends to drain back into the abdominal cavity when the child is lying down, causing the swelling to decrease.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference states fluid 'tends to drain back into the abdominal cavity' when lying down, explaining morning resolution.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct diagnosis but omits or reverses the mechanism of morning resolution.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains resolution by morning; core mechanism of communicating hydrocele.

items.title: Evening worsening from upright posture
items.description: States that the swelling worsens in the evening due to the child being upright or active during the day.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that evening worsening reflects upright posture and fluid tracking down; reference implies this but states it less explicitly.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct diagnosis but does not explain the evening worsening pattern.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains the evening pattern; important supporting reasoning for communicating hydrocele.

items.title: Positional fluid shift
items.description: States that the communicating nature allows fluid to shift based on the child's position.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that diurnal variation is the defining feature pointing to a communicating process via positional fluid shift.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names communicating hydrocele but does not explain why the communicating type is specifically indicated.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Links the communicating nature to positional variation; key mechanistic point.

items.title: Transillumination rules out solid
items.description: States that the positive transillumination test helps distinguish this fluid-filled swelling from solid or bowel pathology such as an inguinal hernia.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that transillumination supports hydrocele over solid or bowel-containing pathology.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions transillumination but does not connect it to ruling out the key differential of hernia.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds differential diagnosis depth; real but secondary to the core reasoning.

items.title: Patent processus vaginalis
items.description: States that a patent processus vaginalis connects the abdominal cavity to the scrotal sac, allowing fluid to shift between them.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that the underlying embryologic mechanism is a patent processus vaginalis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct diagnosis but does not identify the anatomic mechanism of communication.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Anatomical mechanism adds depth; not required to reach the correct diagnosis.

items.title: Avoids non-communicating label
items.description: Avoids diagnosing a non-communicating hydrocele instead of a communicating hydrocele despite the swelling that resolves by morning and recurs.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that non-communicating hydrocele would persist regardless of position and not fluctuate diurnally.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct diagnosis but does not justify why the non-communicating type is excluded.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly tests the key diagnostic distinction; diurnal variation rules out non-communicating type.

items.title: Avoids reversed fluid direction
items.description: Avoids reversing the direction of fluid shift by claiming that lying down causes fluid to accumulate in the scrotum rather than drain back into the abdominal cavity.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Causal direction of resolution' — the direction of fluid shift through a patent processus vaginalis is easy to invert if gravity is reasoned about loosely.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct diagnosis but states that supine posture causes scrotal fluid accumulation rather than drainage back to the abdomen.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specific mechanistic error; would undermine the explanation for morning resolution.

items.title: Selects Mercury option
items.description: The response identifies option A. mercury as the poisoning agent that causes acrodynia, also known as pink disease.

provenance.evidence_detail: Sub-question (a) requires selecting the correct MCQ option; the reference answer states A. Mercury.
provenance.discriminates: A response that selects B, C, or D or fails to commit to a single option.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core MCQ answer; without selecting mercury the response is simply wrong.

items.title: States mercury causation
items.description: The response explicitly states that acrodynia (pink disease) occurs in mercury poisoning.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference answer and all three rollouts agree that acrodynia/Pink disease is caused by mercury poisoning.
provenance.discriminates: A response that picks the correct letter but gives a wrong or absent causative agent in its explanation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Reinforces the correct answer with the named disease and poisoning agent link.

items.title: Specifies inorganic mercury
items.description: The response mentions that acrodynia is associated with inorganic or mercurous mercury (e.g., calomel in teething powders) rather than organic mercury.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Wrong mercury species' notes acrodynia is specifically linked to inorganic/mercurous mercury.
provenance.discriminates: A response that dismisses mercury because it assumes mercury syndromes are limited to methylmercury/Minamata disease.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds pharmacological specificity distinguishing acrodynia from Minamata disease.

items.title: Distinguishes arsenic signs
items.description: The response notes that arsenic poisoning produces cutaneous signs such as hyperpigmentation, keratosis, or Mee's lines, distinguishing these from acrodynia.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts agree arsenic causes hyperpigmentation, keratosis, and Mee's lines, not acrodynia.
provenance.discriminates: A response that conflates arsenic skin toxicity with the pink extremity syndrome of acrodynia.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Clarifies why arsenic is not the correct answer by naming its distinct features.

items.title: Distinguishes thallium signs
items.description: The response notes that thallium poisoning produces alopecia and painful peripheral neuropathy, distinguishing these from pink disease.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts agree thallium causes alopecia and painful neuropathy, not acrodynia.
provenance.discriminates: A response that confuses thallium's painful extremity neuropathy with acrodynia's painful pink hands and feet.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Clarifies why thallium is not the correct answer by naming its distinct features.

items.title: Distinguishes lead signs
items.description: The response notes that lead poisoning produces encephalopathy, colic, or basophilic stippling rather than acrodynia.

provenance.evidence_detail: All three rollouts agree lead causes colic, encephalopathy, and basophilic stippling, not acrodynia.
provenance.discriminates: A response that links the pediatric nature of acrodynia to childhood lead poisoning instead of mercury.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Minor depth distinguishing lead from the acrodynia-causing agent.

items.title: Names extinction
items.description: The response identifies extinction as the psychological process that best explains why the 7-year-old patient stopped crying before physician visits.

provenance.evidence_detail: The single required deliverable is naming the psychological process; the reference and all rollouts identify extinction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names habituation, counterconditioning, desensitization, or forgetting instead of extinction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without naming extinction the response fails entirely.

items.title: Crying as conditioned response
items.description: The response states that the child's crying was a conditioned response developed through negative associations with prior medical experiences.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus claim states: 'crying (CR)' is the conditioned response that diminishes during extinction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction but does not specify which behavior was the conditioned response.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key framing that establishes the learned fear response undergoing extinction.

items.title: Extinction defined
items.description: The response defines extinction as the process by which a conditioned response diminishes because the expected negative outcome no longer occurs.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states: 'Extinction occurs when the conditioned response, in this case, the crying, diminishes because the expected negative outcome no longer occurs.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction without stating what the process entails.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Demonstrates understanding of the mechanism rather than merely naming the term.

items.title: Non-reinforced exposure mechanism
items.description: The response explains that extinction occurred because repeated physician visits no longer produced the expected negative outcome, weakening the conditioned association.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Unanswered mechanism linkage' (severity low) warns that a bare label 'extinction' without mapping to conditioning elements is insufficient.
provenance.discriminates: A response that provides only the bare label 'extinction' with no connection to the physician-visit scenario.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects the definition to the specific vignette elements and causal chain.

items.title: Visits became routine
items.description: The response states that physician visits became routine and devoid of negative experiences over time, causing the association to weaken.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference states: 'as the visits became routine and devoid of negative experiences,' language no rollout used.
provenance.discriminates: A response that explains extinction mechanistically but omits the temporal/familiarity dimension of visits becoming routine.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Anchors the mechanism in the temporal progression described in the vignette.

items.title: Fear reduced
items.description: The response states that the child's fear of physician visits has been reduced, leading to the cessation of crying behavior.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference concludes: 'the child's fear of doctor visits has reduced, leading to the cessation of the crying behavior.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that identifies extinction but does not connect the process to the emotional outcome of reduced fear.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Names the emotional outcome of extinction and links it to behavior change.

items.title: No rewards needed
items.description: The response explicitly notes that the cessation of crying occurred without reward contingencies, distinguishing extinction from positive reinforcement.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed cessation occurred without rewards; the reference and question emphasize 'even without the promise of rewards.'
provenance.discriminates: A response that attributes the behavioral change to rewards, praise, or positive reinforcement.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Uses vignette detail to rule out reinforcement; absorbs the positive-reinforcement pitfall.

items.title: CS identified
items.description: The response identifies the physician visit as the conditioned stimulus that had been associated with negative medical experiences.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus claim states: 'physician visits (CS) associated with aversive medical experiences (US).'
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction but does not map the conditioning elements to the vignette.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds precision to the classical conditioning framework without being essential.

items.title: US identified
items.description: The response identifies the prior negative medical experiences as the unconditioned stimulus that originally elicited crying.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus claim states: 'physician visits (CS) associated with aversive medical experiences (US), producing crying (CR).'
provenance.discriminates: A response that names extinction but does not specify what the original aversive stimulus was.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds precision to the classical conditioning framework without being essential.

items.title: Avoids operant framing
items.description: Avoids framing the crying as an operant behavior reinforced by attention or escape, and instead identifies the process as classical Pavlovian extinction of a conditioned fear response.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Operant extinction confusion' warns that crying can be misread as an operant behavior maintained by attention.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels the process as operant extinction or claims crying was previously reinforced by attention.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Critical conceptual distinction; operant mischaracterization would invalidate the explanation.

items.title: Avoids counterconditioning
items.description: Avoids naming counterconditioning as the psychological process, since the cessation occurred without the promise of rewards and without pairing the feared stimulus with a new positive association.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Counterconditioning claim' (severity high) warns that counterconditioning requires an active positive replacement, which the vignette rules out.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers 'counterconditioning,' implying a new positive association was formed to replace the negative one.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common false lead given the no-rewards detail; directly contradicted by vignette.

items.title: Avoids other wrong labels
items.description: Avoids naming habituation, systematic desensitization, forgetting, or spontaneous recovery as the psychological process, and instead identifies extinction as the weakening of the learned conditioned crying response.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Habituation vs extinction' (severity high) warns that habituation sounds plausible but applies to unconditioned responses, not learned fear associations.
provenance.discriminates: A response that answers 'habituation,' treating the diminished crying as a decreased innate response rather than weakening of a conditioned response.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Consolidates multiple incorrect process labels that would undermine the answer.

items.title: Fetal renal abnormality
items.description: The response identifies a fetal renal abnormality as the condition most likely associated with the reduced amniotic fluid volume at 30 weeks, framing the cause as fetal in origin rather than maternal.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed the cause is fetal/renal; the reference consistently frames the answer as a fetal condition.
provenance.discriminates: A response that attributes the low AFI primarily to a maternal condition rather than a fetal renal abnormality.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without it the response is fundamentally wrong.

items.title: Bilateral renal agenesis named
items.description: The response names bilateral renal agenesis as a specific fetal condition causing the reduced amniotic fluid volume.

provenance.evidence_detail: Rollouts disagreed on specificity; the reference explicitly names bilateral renal agenesis as a cause.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions only a vague 'kidney problem' without naming bilateral renal agenesis or a comparable specific fetal renal entity.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key specific diagnosis directly from the reference answer.

items.title: Urinary tract obstruction named
items.description: The response names urinary tract obstruction, such as posterior urethral valves, as a specific fetal cause of the reduced amniotic fluid volume.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference presents urinary tract obstructions as a co-equal cause; rollouts mentioned obstructions only in differentials, if at all.
provenance.discriminates: A response limited solely to bilateral renal agenesis that omits urinary tract obstruction as a qualifying cause.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Required co-equal example from the reference answer.

items.title: Impeded urine output mechanism
items.description: The response explains that bilateral renal agenesis or urinary tract obstruction impede fetal urine output, leading to oligohydramnios.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly states that these conditions impede fetal urine output, leading to oligohydramnios.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names the condition but does not connect it mechanistically to reduced fetal urine output.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Connects the diagnosis to the pathophysiology of reduced volume.

items.title: Fetal urine as fluid source
items.description: The response states that at 30 weeks the fetus contributes to amniotic fluid volume through urine production, anchoring the gestational age to the reasoning.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts agreed that fetal urine is the major source at 30 weeks; the reference anchors the answer to this physiology.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives the correct diagnosis without any physiological linkage to fetal urine production at 30 weeks.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains why a renal cause is most likely at this gestational age.

items.title: AFI 4 cm is oligohydramnios
items.description: The response states that an AFI of 4 cm meets the definition of oligohydramnios.

provenance.evidence_detail: The consensus_correct block records that AFI ≤5 cm defines oligohydramnios and the patient's AFI is 4 cm.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats the AFI of 4 cm as normal or fails to recognize it as oligohydramnios.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Frames the threshold value that defines the clinical problem.

items.title: Avoids wrong categories
items.description: Avoids selecting post-term pregnancy, which is impossible at 30 weeks, or a cause of polyhydramnios such as maternal diabetes, fetal GI obstruction, or neural tube defect as the associated condition for the low AFI of 4 cm.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Post-term as cause' with high severity; post-term is a classic exam distractor but impossible at 30 weeks.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names post-term pregnancy (≥41 weeks) as the cause of the low AFI at 30 weeks.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Clear-cut category errors that no correct response should make.

items.title: Avoids unsupported alternatives
items.description: Avoids selecting PPROM or placental insufficiency as the most likely cause when the question stem provides no evidence of membrane rupture and specifies 30 weeks with an AFI of 4 cm.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'PPROM selected prematurely' with medium severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that defaults to PPROM as the cause without any mention of ruptured membranes in the stem.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common distractors that are plausible but unsupported by the stem.

items.title: Avoids reversed Potter causality
items.description: If Potter syndrome is mentioned, the response frames it as a consequence of bilateral renal agenesis and reduced fetal urine, not as the cause of the oligohydramnios.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall 'Causal direction reversed' with medium severity.
provenance.discriminates: A response that states Potter syndrome is the cause of the low AFI rather than a downstream consequence.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Niche causal-direction check; adds depth if triggered.

items.title: Renal abnormality as category
items.description: The response uses the term 'renal abnormality' or equivalent categorical language for the fetal condition, rather than relying solely on a single named diagnosis such as bilateral renal agenesis.

provenance.evidence_detail: The single labelled sub-question asks for the most likely associated condition; the reference answer names fetal renal abnormality as the answer.
provenance.discriminates: A response that names placental insufficiency, maternal dehydration, or post-term pregnancy instead of a fetal renal cause.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Categorical phrasing matches the reference answer's framing.

items.title: Identifies Jarisch-Herxheimer
items.description: The response identifies the reaction as a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in this 24-year-old with secondary syphilis after receiving intramuscular benzathine penicillin.

provenance.evidence_detail: Core deliverable of the question: identify the reaction and state management.
provenance.discriminates: A response that labels it an allergic reaction or serum sickness without naming Jarisch-Herxheimer.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core diagnosis; without it, management reasoning is ungrounded.

items.title: Supportive care next step
items.description: The response states that the most next step in management is supportive care for the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference answer states management involves supportive care.
provenance.discriminates: A response that recommends epinephrine, steroids, antihistamines, or switching antibiotics instead of supportive care.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Directly answers the question; correctness depends on this.

items.title: Antipyretics named
items.description: The response names antipyretics such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen to alleviate fever, headache, and muscle aches as part of supportive care for the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference explicitly names acetaminophen or ibuprofen; rollouts only mentioned acetaminophen.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives only antihistamines or steroids without mentioning antipyretics.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Specifies the concrete intervention; central to correct management.

items.title: Not penicillin allergy
items.description: The response states that this is not an allergic reaction to penicillin, supported by the absence of bronchospasm, and avoids labeling the patient as having a penicillin allergy.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that JHR is not anaphylaxis; the question explicitly notes no bronchospasm.
provenance.discriminates: A response that classifies the reaction as penicillin allergy or anaphylaxis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correctly distinguishes JHR from anaphylaxis; prevents wrong pathway.

items.title: Continue penicillin therapy
items.description: The response indicates that benzathine penicillin therapy should not be stopped or switched because the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is not a contraindication to continuing treatment.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall: stops or switches antibiotic.
provenance.discriminates: A response that recommends discontinuing penicillin or switching to doxycycline or azithromycin.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Critical management decision; stopping therapy is a common error.

items.title: Self-limited within 24 hours
items.description: The response states that the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is generally self-limited, usually resolves within 24 hours, and is not dangerous.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference states symptoms resolve on their own within 24 hours.
provenance.discriminates: A response that implies prolonged course requiring escalation or hospital admission.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Prognosis informs management decisions; supports supportive care.

items.title: Monitoring mentioned
items.description: The response mentions monitoring the patient to ensure no other complications arise from the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference explicitly states monitoring is important; no rollout included it.
provenance.discriminates: A response that gives no follow-up or monitoring guidance at all.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Adds clinical depth; real but secondary to the core management.

items.title: Onset timing consistent
items.description: The response recognizes that symptom onset 8 hours after intramuscular benzathine penicillin is consistent with a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction rather than serum sickness.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall: confuses with serum sickness, which occurs 7-10 days post-exposure.
provenance.discriminates: A response that diagnoses serum sickness based on this 8-hour onset.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Supports correct diagnosis through timing; useful reasoning.

items.title: Common in secondary syphilis
items.description: The response notes that the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is especially common after initiating antibiotic treatment for secondary syphilis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Reference states JHR is common especially in secondary syphilis.
provenance.discriminates: A response that does not connect the reaction to the specific diagnosis of secondary syphilis.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Contextual depth; reinforces correct diagnosis.

items.title: Avoids epinephrine
items.description: Avoids recommending epinephrine for this reaction, since the 24-year-old has no bronchospasm and this is a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, not anaphylaxis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall: misclassifies as anaphylaxis and gives epinephrine IM.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats fever and chills after penicillin as anaphylaxis and administers epinephrine.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Common dangerous mistake observed; high clinical significance.

items.title: Avoids allergy-directed treatment
items.description: Avoids recommending systemic corticosteroids, antihistamines, or hospital admission for this uncomplicated Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in secondary syphilis.

provenance.evidence_detail: Mined pitfall: gives corticosteroids for JHR.
provenance.discriminates: A response that prescribes steroids for a self-limited reaction.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Treating JHR as allergy is a frequent observed error; avoids overtreatment.

items.title: Mastectomy as strategy
items.description: States mastectomy as the management strategy for the 45-year-old patient with diffuse microcalcifications and biopsy-confirmed DCIS.

provenance.evidence_detail: The question asks for the most appropriate management strategy; the reference answer identifies mastectomy.
provenance.discriminates: A response that recommends lumpectomy, observation, or any non-surgical approach as the primary strategy.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Core answer; without mastectomy the response fails entirely.

items.title: Diffuse calcifications preclude lumpectomy
items.description: States that the diffuse microcalcifications on mammography indicate widespread or multifocal disease, making lumpectomy unable to remove all affected areas.

provenance.evidence_detail: All correct rollouts and the reference agree that diffuse microcalcifications preclude breast-conserving surgery; this is the core clinical rationale.
provenance.discriminates: A response that recommends mastectomy but justifies it solely on family history without mentioning that diffuse disease prevents lumpectomy.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Key reasoning driving surgical choice; absorbed the avoidance restatement of lumpectomy.

items.title: Identifies DCIS diagnosis
items.description: Identifies the biopsy-confirmed diagnosis as intraductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) rather than invasive breast cancer.

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that the diagnosis is DCIS; correctly recognizing the in situ nature prevents invasive-cancer management errors.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats the carcinoma as invasive or fails to acknowledge the in situ designation.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Correct disease classification is required for correct management selection.

items.title: Family history as supporting factor
items.description: Mentions family history of breast carcinoma as a supporting factor for choosing mastectomy over breast-conserving surgery.

provenance.evidence_detail: All rollouts and the reference mention family history as reinforcing the surgical approach, though it is secondary to disease extent.
provenance.discriminates: A response that omits family history entirely from the rationale or treats it as irrelevant.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Salient clinical detail reinforcing surgical decision; moderate discrimination expected.

items.title: Reduces future cancer risk
items.description: States that mastectomy would reduce the risk of future breast cancer considering the family history.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly states that mastectomy reduces the risk of future breast cancer; rollouts mention family history raising risk but do not all articulate risk reduction.
provenance.discriminates: A response that mentions family history but does not connect it to future risk reduction from mastectomy.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Explains prophylactic benefit; distinct from merely naming family history.

items.title: Genetic counseling mentioned
items.description: Includes genetic counseling as part of the decision-making process given the family history of breast cancer.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly frames genetic counseling as an important part of the decision-making process; rollouts mention it in passing but do not emphasize it.
provenance.discriminates: A response that addresses only the surgical decision without mentioning genetic counseling.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Real added depth from reference answer; not essential to core management choice.

items.title: Reconstructive surgery discussed
items.description: Includes reconstructive surgery options as part of the discussions with the healthcare team regarding mastectomy.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference mentions reconstructive surgery options as an important part of the decision-making process; no rollout mentions it.
provenance.discriminates: A response that focuses solely on the surgical indication without addressing reconstructive options.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Practical adjunct from reference answer; low discrimination but clinically relevant.

items.title: Current and future management
items.description: States that the management strategy addresses both the current DCIS and future risk factors.

provenance.evidence_detail: The reference explicitly frames mastectomy as addressing both current DCIS and future risk factors; rollouts address these separately but do not synthesize them.
provenance.discriminates: A response that addresses only the current disease without acknowledging future risk management.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Synthesis statement from reference answer; minor added depth.

items.title: Avoids observation-only
items.description: Avoids recommending mammographic surveillance or observation without surgery for the biopsy-confirmed DCIS with diffuse microcalcifications.

provenance.evidence_detail: Medium-severity mined pitfall: some literature debates overdiagnosis of low-grade DCIS, potentially leading to undertreatment of extensive disease.
provenance.discriminates: A response that recommends close surveillance rather than surgical management because DCIS is non-invasive.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Dangerous under-treatment trap; the diffuse disease mandates surgical management.

items.title: Avoids family history as sole driver
items.description: Avoids justifying mastectomy primarily on family history rather than on the diffuse microcalcifications indicating extensive disease.

provenance.evidence_detail: Medium-severity mined pitfall: family history is emotionally salient and linked to prophylactic mastectomy narratives, but the primary indication here is disease extent.
provenance.discriminates: A response that frames the mastectomy as a prophylactic decision driven by family history rather than as therapeutic for diffuse DCIS.
provenance.calibration_rationale: Reasoning trap; correct rationale centers on diffuse disease extent, not family history alone.

items.title: Identifies DCIS diagnosis
items.description: Identifies the biopsy-confirmed diagnosis as intraductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS).

provenance.evidence_detail: Consensus among rollouts that the diagnosis is DCIS; correctly recognizing the in situ nature prevents invasive-cancer management errors.
provenance.discriminates: A response that treats the carcinoma as invasive or fails to acknowledge the in situ designation.
